Also in *al-Sihah*: *nafaḥat al-nāqa* means she struck with her leg; *nafahahu bi-l-sayf* means he took it up. (ʿA)]. He saw Iblis speaking with 'Isa (peace be upon him) on some mountain of the holy land, so he struck him with his wing, a blow that cast him to the farthest mountain in India.

﴿Possessed of power﴾: possessed of soundness of intellect [*ḥaṣāfa fī 'aqlihi*, meaning firmness. This is according to *al-Sihah*. (ʿA)] and judgment, and firmness in his religion.

﴿Then he stood﴾: he stood upright in his true form, not in the form he used to take whenever he descended with revelation. He used to descend in the form of Dihya. That is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) loved to see him in the form in which he was created, so he appeared to him on the highest horizon, which is the horizon of the sun, and filled the horizon. [I have not found it in this form. In the two *Sahihs*, from the narration of Masruq from 'A'isha: "I was the first to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said, 'It is only Jibril. I did not see him in his form in which you saw him except these two times: I saw him descending from heaven, filling the expanse between heaven and earth with the greatness of his form.'" In al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Hibban: "But he saw Jibril; he did not see him in his form except twice: once at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, and once at Ajyad. He had six hundred wings, and he had filled the horizon."]

It is said: no prophet saw him in his true form except Muhammad (ﷺ), twice: once on earth and once in heaven. [I have not found this as stated. As for mentioning the two times, it was mentioned in the previous report.]

﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾: he approached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and was suspended in the air above him. From this comes *tadallat al-thamara* (the fruit hung down), and *dallā rijlayhi min al-sarīr* (he let his legs hang down from the bed).

*Al-dawālī* are the hanging fruits. A poet said:

*He hung down over them between a rope and a cord, hanging like the bucket of a drawing man, shaking.* [This line is attributed to Abu Dhu'ayb, the second half being: "with a bare mare like a leather mat, whose rider stumbles." *Al-sabb*, with a kasra, is a rope, a headband, or a turban. *Al-khayṭa* is likewise, meaning a peg or the like, in the dialect of Hudhayl. *Al-mā'iḥ* is the one who fills the bucket from the bottom of the well. *Al-māʾiḥ* (with a *ta'*) is the one who draws water. The poet describes the one who gathers honey as hanging over the bees or the honey, because it is also feminine. That is, he descended holding onto a rope fastened to a peg, like the bucket of an energetic filler. *Al-jardā'* is a mare with little hair. *Al-wakf* is a leather mat. *Kabā al-jawād yakbū* means it fell on its face. *Ghurāb al-dābba* is the upper part of its back, meaning that its back seems to slope because of the speed of its gait.]

It is said: he is like the *qarlā* [the kite? (a bird)]: if he sees good, he descends, and if he does not see it, he turns away.

*Qāba qawsayn*: the measure of two Arab bows. *Al-qāb*, *al-qayb*, *al-qād*, *al-qayd*, and *al-qays* all mean measure. Zayd ibn 'Ali read *qād*, and *qīd* and *qadr* are also read. Measurement has been given by the bow, the spear, the whip, the forearm, the arm's span, the stride, the handspan, the span of the fingers, and the finger. From this is the saying: "No prayer until the sun has risen to the measure of two spears." [Al-Hakim related it from the report of 'Amr ibn 'Abasa in a long hadith; Ishaq and al-Daraqutni related it from the report of Ka'b ibn Murra similarly, in a hadith; al-Tabarani related it from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf in brief.] In the hadith: "The space of the bow of one of you in Paradise, and the place of his whip, is better than the world and what is in it." [Al-Bukhari related it through Humayd from Anas, more complete than this.] *Al-qadd* is the whip.

It is said: there is a short distance between them. A poet said:

*And you have made me from Huzayma a finger's breadth.* [*Fa-adraka ibqā' al-'arāwa zal'ahā, wa qad ja'altanī min Huzayma iṣba'an*

This is by al-Kalhiyya, and it is a nickname of 'Abd Allah ibn Hubayra. It is also said to be Jarir ibn Hubayra, or Hubayra ibn 'Abd Manaf. It is also said to be by al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur, or Ru'ba, but this is nothing. *Al-ibqā'* is what the mare retains of her energy to spend near the reaching of the goal. *Al-'arāwa* is like *jarāda*; it is also said that with a kasra it is the name of his mare. *Al-zal'* (with a fatha) is a limp in gait from pain in the leg. Meaning: the limp overtook what the mare had retained, so she could not spend it, while she had made me close to my enemy Huzayma (with an unpointed *ha*, then a pointed *kasra*), a man who had raided the poet's camels and then been pursued by him. It is also said that it is his tribe, but this is not so. Another version reads *fa-adraka irqāl al-'arāwa*. *Al-irqāl* is hastening in movement, meaning that the limp nullified her speed. We must interpret his words "you made me a finger", meaning: you made me one whose distance is a finger's breadth, or you made my distance the measure of a finger.]

If you say: how is the measure in His words *fa-kāna qāba qawsayn*? I say: the measure is "the distance of his nearness was like the measure of two bows." [Mahmud said: "Its measure: the distance of his nearness was like the measure of two bows," to the end. Ahmad said: Some of them have said it is a metaphor for a covenant to adhere to obedience, because when two allies in Arab custom pledge themselves to loyalty and purity, they press together and their two bows are joined. Ahmad said: in this there is an inclination toward His words *aw adnā*.]

So these added terms are omitted, as Abu 'Ali said in his line:

*And you have made me from Huzayma a finger's breadth.*

That is: one with the measure of the distance of a finger's breadth. *Aw adnā*: that is, according to your estimate, like His words *aw yazīdūn* (or they increase). *Ilā 'abdihi*: to His servant, that is, to the servant of Allah, though no mention of His name has preceded, because there is no ambiguity, like His words *'alā ẓahrihā* (upon its back).

*Mā awḥā*: a glorification of the revelation that was revealed. [Mahmud said: "This is a glorification of the revelation that Allah revealed to him." Ahmad said: the glorification is because of what it contains of vagueness, as if it were too great to be encompassed by explanation. It is like His words *idh yaghshā al-sidrata mā yaghshā* and His words *fa-ghashiyahum min al-yammi mā ghashiyahum*.]

Its meaning: it was said that he was revealed: "Paradise is forbidden to the prophets until you enter it, and to the nations until your nation enters it."

﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾: the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not deny what his eyes saw of the form of Jibril (peace be upon him). That is, his heart did not say, when he saw it: "I do not recognize you," for had it said that, it would have been lying, because he recognized him. The meaning is that he saw him with his eyes and recognized him with his heart, and he did not doubt that what he saw was true. It is also read *mā kadhaba*, meaning that he confirmed it, and did not doubt that it was Jibril (peace be upon him) in his form.

﴿Will you dispute with him what he saw?﴾: from *al-mirā'*, which is contention and argument. Its derivation is from *maraya al-nāqa* (he milked the she-camel), as if each of the two disputants milks what is with his companion. It is also read *afa-tamrūnahu*, meaning: will you overcome him in disputation, from *mārayatuhu fa-maraytuhu*. Because of the meaning of victory in it, it is construed with *'alā*, as you say "I overcame him in such-and-such." It is also said that *afa-tamrūnahu* means: will you deny him. They have recited:

*If you revile a brother of truth and nobility, you have indeed milked a brother who was not one to be milked by you.* [He says to his companion: if you blame a brother of truth and nobility, meaning himself. It is said: *maraya al-nāqa*, meaning he milked her. From this comes *al-mirā'*, as if each of the two disputants milks what is with his companion. From it: "you have indeed contended with a brother of truth," meaning you overcame him in dispute and drew out what was with him, because whoever milks a she-camel leaves her udder dry, or you denied his right as if you had taken it from him, or you caused what was with him to come out, so he blames you as you blamed him. *Mā kāna yumrīka*, meaning: what he did not do to you like that.]

They also said: it is said *mariyatuhu ḥaqqahu* when you deny it. Its construction with *'alā* is valid only according to the doctrine of implication (*taḍmīn*).

﴿Another descent﴾: a second time of descending. The word *nazla* is put in the accusative in the manner of the adverb of time, which is "once", because the form *fa'la* is a noun for the single occurrence of the verb, so it has its ruling. That is: Jibril (peace be upon him) descended upon him a second descent in his own form, and he saw him in it. That was on the night of the Ascension (*mi'rāj*).

It is said about the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (*sidrat al-muntahā*): it is a jujube tree in the seventh heaven, to the right of the Throne. Its fruit is like the jars of Hajar, and its leaves are like the ears of elephants. From its root flow the rivers which Allah mentioned in His Book. A rider walks in its shade for seventy years without crossing it.

*Al-muntahā* means the place of ending, or the ending itself, as if it were at the furthest limit and end of Paradise. It is also said: no one has passed beyond it, and to it the knowledge of the angels and others ends, and no one knows what is beyond it. It is also said: the spirits of the martyrs terminate there.

﴿The Garden of Refuge﴾: the Garden to which the God-fearing go. Thus related al-Hasan. It is also said: the spirits of the martyrs take refuge in it.

And Ali and Ibn al-Zubayr and a group [of readers] recited: jannatu l-ma'wa (the Garden of Refuge), meaning: it covered it with its shadows and entered into it. It is reported from Aisha that she rejected this reading and said: "Whoever recites it that way, may God cover him [with a curse]." [Cf. the Arabic phrase: fa-ajannahu Allah.] "...what covered it" is an expression of magnification and amplification of what covered it. By this expression it is known that what covered it of creatures indicating the greatness and majesty of God are things that description cannot fathom and attribute cannot encompass. It has also been said: a vast multitude of angels covered it, worshipping God in its presence. And it is reported from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I saw on every leaf of it an angel standing, glorifying God." [Narrated by al-Tabari through the route of Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: it was said to him, "O Messenger of God, what did you see covering that tree?" and he mentioned it and completed it more than this. But Abd al-Rahman is weak, and this report is mu'dal (with two or more consecutive omissions in its chain).] And from him, peace be upon him: it was covered by a canopy (rafraf) of green birds. [I have not found it.] And from Ibn Mas'ud and others: it was covered by golden butterflies (farash min dhahab). [As for the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh narrated it through the route of Murrah from him with this wording and more. As for others, it was narrated by [blank space in the original].]

"His gaze did not swerve, nor did it transgress" (ma zaagha basaru Rasul Allah (ﷺ) wa ma taghaa): that is, he affirmed what he saw with certain and correct affirmation, without his gaze deviating from it or passing beyond it; or: he did not turn away from the wonders he was commanded to see and was enabled to see, and "nor did it transgress" means he did not go beyond what he was commanded to see.

"Indeed he saw of the signs of his Lord the greatest signs" (La-qad ra'a min ayati Rabbihi al-kubra): by God, he indeed saw of the signs of his Lord the signs that are greatest and most magnificent. [Mahmud said: "its meaning is: he indeed saw of the signs of his Lord the signs which..." etc. Ahmad says: It is possible that "the greatest" is an attribute of "signs of his Lord," not a direct object, and the seen object is omitted for magnifying and glorifying the matter, as if he said: "He indeed saw of the greatest signs of his Lord matters of great magnitude that description cannot encompass," and omission in such a case is more eloquent and awe-inspiring. This—and God knows best—is preferable to the first, because in it there is magnification of God's greatest signs, and that among them are what he saw and what he did not see. On the first interpretation, its implication would be that he saw all the greatest signs in totality and generality, and this is far-fetched, for no one can comprehensively know the totality of God's signs. If one says: it is a general term intended as a particular, then it returns to the interpretation we mentioned, and God knows best.]

That is, when he ascended to his Lord to the heavens, and was shown the wonders of the dominion (malakut).

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 53, verses 1–18 (part 1 of 2)**

Meccan [except verse 32, which is Medinan]. Its verses number 62, and it is said 61. [It was revealed after Surah al-Ikhlas.]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

*al-Najm* (the Star): the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), which is its dominant name. A poet said:

*When the Najm rises at night, the shepherd seeks a cloak.* [The Arabs say this about winter. About summer they say:

*When the Najm rises in the morning, the shepherd seeks a waterskin.*

*Al-Najm* is a name dominant over the Pleiades. It is said that it stays hidden for forty days in the year, its light concealed by the sun, and it appears at nightfall when winter begins and at dawn when summer begins. *Al-kisa'* (cloak) is a full garment. *Al-ghadiyya* is the diminutive of *ghadwa*, which is the early part of the day. *Al-shukiyya* is the diminutive of *shukwa*, which is a small, bare waterskin. In winter one seeks a thick cloak because of the great cold, and in summer one seeks a waterskin to drink from because of the great heat. The first is a metaphor for the arrival of cold, and the second for the arrival of heat.]

Or *al-najm* means the genus of stars. A poet said:

*Then she spent the night counting the stars in a restless state.* [They knew that I fulfilled my duty to its owner, so he set out on a hard she-camel, leading another beside her.

I hosted al-Kilabi, who sought hospitality, and your mother, when her camel was driven toward us.

So she spent the night counting the stars in a restless state, a swift one, whose ready contents were consumed by the eaters.

When we gave her the *'akis* (a mixture of broth and milk), she was filled, and her throat-veins swelled and trembled.

When she had satisfied a need from the vessel, she wanted from us a need we did not want.]

This is by al-Ra'i al-Numayri, of Banu Qutn ibn Rabi'a. Guests from Banu Kilab came to him while his camels were away, so he slaughtered for them one of their own riding camels. When morning came, his camels returned to him, so he gave the owner of the slaughtered camel its equivalent, plus an extra female camel in addition to it. Khanzar ibn Arqam of Banu Badr ibn Rabi'a blamed him for slaughtering it, and al-Ra'i replied with a poem containing this verse. *Al-'anas* is a hard she-camel. *Ummuka* is in apposition to *al-Kilabi*.

*Yuhda* is in the passive voice, meaning that she is driven onward with singing. *Al-qu'ud* (like *sabur*) is a young female camel, because a rider cannot sit on her back. Another version reads *idh yuhda ilayka* ("when she is driven toward you") instead of *ilaynā* ("toward us"). Perhaps this comes after the hospitality mentioned later, or it is a distortion.

*Fa-bata ummuka ta'udd al-najm*: she spent the night counting the forms of the stars, or counting the bubbles of broth in the bowl. He therefore uses *al-najm* as a metaphor in the form of explicit metaphor (*al-tasrihiyya*).

Or she counts the Pleiades, since *al-najm* is dominant over them, and they are seven stars whose shape is seen on winter nights. It is also said that *al-ʿadd* here means supposing, so that she spent the night supposing about it.

*Al-mustahira* means the one bewildered by being filled with broth. It is also transmitted as *mustajira*, because it draws people to eat from it. *Al-'akis* is broth mixed with fresh milk. *Tamallat* means became full. Another version reads *tamadhdhat* with a non-dotted *dhal*, meaning expanded from being satisfied. Another version reads it with a dotted letter, meaning knocked together and agitated. *Al-madhakhir* are the places of stores, meaning the stomach and intestines. Another version reads *khawasir*, meaning its sides. *Irtafad* means dripped, sprinkled, trembled, and fled. Another version reads *wazdada rashhan wariduha* (its veins increased in sweat).

The meaning is: she spent the night looking at the stars in a bowl abundant with broth and fat, whose fat quickly congealed in the hands of the eaters because of the winter cold. Until, when her belly was full and the veins of her neck were distended, and she had satisfied a need from the owner of the vessel (which is the broth and milk), she asked us for something we did not want or accept, because it was excessive. It is as if she intended the meaning of supplication, inclination, or relation, so he used *ila* after it. It is also permissible that *ila* means *min* (from), as we have explained at the end of the letter *ba'*.

*Yurid al-nujum idha hawa*: he means the stars when they set, or when they are scattered on the Day of Resurrection. Or *al-najm* is the star by which the devils are stoned, when it falls, or when it plunges down. Or *al-najm* is one of the stars of the Qur'an, which was sent down in portions over twenty years. *Idha hawa* means when it descended. Or *al-nabat* (plants): when it falls, meaning when it drops to the ground.

It is related from 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr that 'Utba ibn Abi Lahab, whose wife was the daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), intended to go out to Syria. He said, "I will go to Muhammad and harm him." He came to him and said, "O Muhammad, he disbelieves in the star when it falls, and in the one who drew near and then descended." Then he spat in the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), returned his daughter to him, and divorced her. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "O Allah, set upon him one of Your dogs." Abu Talib was present, and was stricken with grief [*fawajam lahā*, meaning his grief intensified. This is according to *al-Sihah*. (ʿA)]. He said, "How self-sufficient you would have been, O nephew, from this call!" 'Utba returned to his father and informed him. Then they went out toward Syria and camped at a station. A monk from the monastery overlooked them and said, "This is a land of predators." Abu Lahab said to his companions, "Help us, O company of Quraysh, this night, for I fear for my son because of Muhammad's supplication." So they gathered their camels and made them kneel around them, and they encircled 'Utba. A lion came, sniffing their faces, until it struck 'Utba and killed him. [Abu Nu'aym related it in *al-Dala'il* through Ibn Ishaq, from 'Uthman ibn 'Urwa, from his father, and mentioned something similar, except that he said, "The lion struck him with its tail one blow, and he died on the spot." Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* and al-Tabarani related it through Sa'id from Qatada at length, similar to this. But 'Anbasa said: al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi also related it in *al-Dala'il*, from the narration of Abu Nawfal ibn Abi 'Aqrab from his father, who said, "It was Lahab ibn Abi Lahab," and mentioned it briefly. Al-Bayhaqi said: this is what 'Abbas ibn al-Fadl al-Azraq said, but it is not strong. The people of the military expeditions say it was 'Utba or 'Utayba.]

Hassan said:

*Whoever returns this year to his family, the lion's prey will not return.* [*Lā yarfa'u al-Rahmanu maṣra'akum, wa lā yuwhinu quwwata al-ṣāri'*

*wa kāna fīhi lakum 'ibratun, al-sayyidu al-matbū'u wa al-tābi'*

*man yarji'u al-'ilma ilā ahlihi, fa-mā akīlu al-sab'i bi al-rāji'*

*man 'āda fa-al-layth lahu 'ā'id, a'ẓim bihi min khabar shā'i'*

These are by Hassan ibn Thabit. He related from 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr that 'Utba ibn Abi Lahab had the daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as his wife. He went to him and said, "He disbelieves in the star when it falls, and in the one who drew near and then descended." Then he spat in his face and divorced his daughter and went out to Syria. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "O Allah, set upon him one of Your dogs." Then, one night while they were guarding him on a journey, a lion came, sniffing their faces until it struck 'Utba and killed him. Hassan said this. The two verbs are in the jussive, governed by *lā* of supplication. *Yuwahhin* is with the intensive form, and its meaning is supplication against the slain and supplication for the slayer. *Al-maṣra'* means the one thrown down. *Al-'ibra* means consideration, or that by which one takes a lesson. *Al-tābi'* is in apposition to *al-sayyid*.

Meaning: whoever returns this year to his family, his return does not make another's return obligatory, because the one eaten by a predator does not return, so his family should not wish for his return, given its impossibility and the predator's habit. Then he said: whoever acts like 'Utba, the lion is his enemy. *A'ẓim bihi* is an exclamation form. *Min khabar* is a specification (*tamyīz*) accompanied by *min*. *Shā'i'* means widespread, spreading.]

﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾: the companion means Muhammad (ﷺ). The address is to Quraysh, and this is the answer to the oath. *Al-ḍalāl* is the opposite of guidance, and *al-ghayy* is the opposite of rightness. The meaning is: he is rightly guided and upright, and it is not as you claim when you attribute to him error and deviation. What he has brought you of the Qur'an is not speech issuing from his desire or opinion, but a revelation from Allah that is revealed to him. This verse is used as proof by those who do not consider *ijtihad* (independent reasoning) permissible for prophets. The answer is that when Allah permits them to exercise *ijtihad*, then *ijtihad* and what it rests upon is entirely revelation, not speech from desire.

﴿Taught him by one mighty in power﴾: an angel mighty in power. The genitive construction is not literal, because it is the attributive adjective (*al-ṣifa al-mushabbaha*) construed with its agent, and that is Jibril (peace be upon him). Among his strength: he uprooted the cities of the people of Lut from the black water and carried them on his wing, raised them to heaven, and then overturned them. He shouted a cry at Thamud and they became prostrate in their homes. His descent to the prophets and his ascent were swifter than the return of a glance [*fī awḥā min rij'at al-ṭarf*. (Note: *awḥā* means swifter than the wahy, which is speed; it may be read with madd or qasr. Also in *al-Sihah*: *nafaḥat al-nāqa* means she struck with her leg; *nafahahu bi-l-sayf* means he took it up. (ʿA)]. He saw Iblis speaking with 'Isa (peace be upon him) on some mountain of the holy land, so he struck him with his wing, a blow that cast him to the farthest mountain in India.

﴿Possessed of power﴾: possessed of soundness of intellect [*ḥaṣāfa fī 'aqlihi*, meaning firmness. This is according to *al-Sihah*. (ʿA)] and judgment, and firmness in his religion.

﴿Then he stood﴾: he stood upright in his true form, not in the form he used to take whenever he descended with revelation. He used to descend in the form of Dihya. That is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) loved to see him in the form in which he was created, so he appeared to him on the highest horizon, which is the horizon of the sun, and filled the horizon. [I have not found it in this form. In the two *Sahihs*, from the narration of Masruq from 'A'isha: "I was the first to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said, 'It is only Jibril. I did not see him in his form in which you saw him except these two times: I saw him descending from heaven, filling the expanse between heaven and earth with the greatness of his form.'" In al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Hibban: "But he saw Jibril; he did not see him in his form except twice: once at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, and once at Ajyad. He had six hundred wings, and he had filled the horizon."]

It is said: no prophet saw him in his true form except Muhammad (ﷺ), twice: once on earth and once in heaven. [I have not found this as stated. As for mentioning the two times, it was mentioned in the previous report.]

﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾: he approached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and was suspended in the air above him. From this comes *tadallat al-thamara* (the fruit hung down), and *dallā rijlayhi min al-sarīr* (he let his legs hang down from the bed).

*Al-dawālī* are the hanging fruits. A poet said:

*He hung down over them between a rope and a cord, hanging like the bucket of a drawing man, shaking.* [This line is attributed to Abu Dhu'ayb, the second half being: "with a bare mare like a leather mat, whose rider stumbles." *Al-sabb*, with a kasra, is a rope, a headband, or a turban. *Al-khayṭa* is likewise, meaning a peg or the like, in the dialect of Hudhayl. *Al-mā'iḥ* is the one who fills the bucket from the bottom of the well. *Al-māʾiḥ* (with a *ta'*) is the one who draws water. The poet describes the one who gathers honey as hanging over the bees or the honey, because it is also feminine. That is, he descended holding onto a rope fastened to a peg, like the bucket of an energetic filler. *Al-jardā'* is a mare with little hair. *Al-wakf* is a leather mat. *Kabā al-jawād yakbū* means it fell on its face. *Ghurāb al-dābba* is the upper part of its back, meaning that its back seems to slope because of the speed of its gait.]

It is said: he is like the *qarlā* [the kite? (a bird)]: if he sees good, he descends, and if he does not see it, he turns away.

*Qāba qawsayn*: the measure of two Arab bows. *Al-qāb*, *al-qayb*, *al-qād*, *al-qayd*, and *al-qays* all mean measure. Zayd ibn 'Ali read *qād*, and *qīd* and *qadr* are also read. Measurement has been given by the bow, the spear, the whip, the forearm, the arm's span, the stride, the handspan, the span of the fingers, and the finger. From this is the saying: "No prayer until the sun has risen to the measure of two spears." [Al-Hakim related it from the report of 'Amr ibn 'Abasa in a long hadith; Ishaq and al-Daraqutni related it from the report of Ka'b ibn Murra similarly, in a hadith; al-Tabarani related it from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf in brief.] In the hadith: "The space of the bow of one of you in Paradise, and the place of his whip, is better than the world and what is in it." [Al-Bukhari related it through Humayd from Anas, more complete than this.] *Al-qadd* is the whip.

It is said: there is a short distance between them. A poet said:

*And you have made me from Huzayma a finger's breadth.* [*Fa-adraka ibqā' al-'arāwa zal'ahā, wa qad ja'altanī min Huzayma iṣba'an*

This is by al-Kalhiyya, and it is a nickname of 'Abd Allah ibn Hubayra. It is also said to be Jarir ibn Hubayra, or Hubayra ibn 'Abd Manaf. It is also said to be by al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur, or Ru'ba, but this is nothing. *Al-ibqā'* is what the mare retains of her energy to spend near the reaching of the goal. *Al-'arāwa* is like *jarāda*; it is also said that with a kasra it is the name of his mare. *Al-zal'* (with a fatha) is a limp in gait from pain in the leg. Meaning: the limp overtook what the mare had retained, so she could not spend it, while she had made me close to my enemy Huzayma (with an unpointed *ha*, then a pointed *kasra*), a man who had raided the poet's camels and then been pursued by him. It is also said that it is his tribe, but this is not so. Another version reads *fa-adraka irqāl al-'arāwa*. *Al-irqāl* is hastening in movement, meaning that the limp nullified her speed. We must interpret his words "you made me a finger", meaning: you made me one whose distance is a finger's breadth, or you made my distance the measure of a finger.]

If you say: how is the measure in His words *fa-kāna qāba qawsayn*? I say: the measure is "the distance of his nearness was like the measure of two bows." [Mahmud said: "Its measure: the distance of his nearness was like the measure of two bows," to the end. Ahmad said: Some of them have said it is a metaphor for a covenant to adhere to obedience, because when two allies in Arab custom pledge themselves to loyalty and purity, they press together and their two bows are joined. Ahmad said: in this there is an inclination toward His words *aw adnā*.]

So these added terms are omitted, as Abu 'Ali said in his line:

*And you have made me from Huzayma a finger's breadth.*

That is: one with the measure of the distance of a finger's breadth. *Aw adnā*: that is, according to your estimate, like His words *aw yazīdūn* (or they increase). *Ilā 'abdihi*: to His servant, that is, to the servant of Allah, though no mention of His name has preceded, because there is no ambiguity, like His words *'alā ẓahrihā* (upon its back).

*Mā awḥā*: a glorification of the revelation that was revealed. [Mahmud said: "This is a glorification of the revelation that Allah revealed to him." Ahmad said: the glorification is because of what it contains of vagueness, as if it were too great to be encompassed by explanation. It is like His words *idh yaghshā al-sidrata mā yaghshā* and His words *fa-ghashiyahum min al-yammi mā ghashiyahum*.]

Its meaning: it was said that he was revealed: "Paradise is forbidden to the prophets until you enter it, and to the nations until your nation enters it."

﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾: the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not deny what his eyes saw of the form of Jibril (peace be upon him). That is, his heart did not say, when he saw it: "I do not recognize you," for had it said that, it would have been lying, because he recognized him. The meaning is that he saw him with his eyes and recognized him with his heart, and he did not doubt that what he saw was true. It is also read *mā kadhaba*, meaning that he confirmed it, and did not doubt that it was Jibril (peace be upon him) in his form.

﴿Will you dispute with him what he saw?﴾: from *al-mirā'*, which is contention and argument. Its derivation is from *maraya al-nāqa* (he milked the she-camel), as if each of the two disputants milks what is with his companion. It is also read *afa-tamrūnahu*, meaning: will you overcome him in disputation, from *mārayatuhu fa-maraytuhu*. Because of the meaning of victory in it, it is construed with *'alā*, as you say "I overcame him in such-and-such." It is also said that *afa-tamrūnahu* means: will you deny him. They have recited:

*If you revile a brother of truth and nobility, you have indeed milked a brother who was not one to be milked by you.* [He says to his companion: if you blame a brother of truth and nobility, meaning himself. It is said: *maraya al-nāqa*, meaning he milked her. From this comes *al-mirā'*, as if each of the two disputants milks what is with his companion. From it: "you have indeed contended with a brother of truth," meaning you overcame him in dispute and drew out what was with him, because whoever milks a she-camel leaves her udder dry, or you denied his right as if you had taken it from him, or you caused what was with him to come out, so he blames you as you blamed him. *Mā kāna yumrīka*, meaning: what he did not do to you like that.]

They also said: it is said *mariyatuhu ḥaqqahu* when you deny it. Its construction with *'alā* is valid only according to the doctrine of implication (*taḍmīn*).

﴿Another descent﴾: a second time of descending. The word *nazla* is put in the accusative in the manner of the adverb of time, which is "once", because the form *fa'la* is a noun for the single occurrence of the verb, so it has its ruling. That is: Jibril (peace be upon him) descended upon him a second descent in his own form, and he saw him in it. That was on the night of the Ascension (*mi'rāj*).

It is said about the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (*sidrat al-muntahā*): it is a jujube tree in the seventh heaven, to the right of the Throne. Its fruit is like the jars of Hajar, and its leaves are like the ears of elephants. From its root flow the rivers which Allah mentioned in His Book. A rider walks in its shade for seventy years without crossing it.

*Al-muntahā* means the place of ending, or the ending itself, as if it were at the furthest limit and end of Paradise. It is also said: no one has passed beyond it, and to it the knowledge of the angels and others ends, and no one knows what is beyond it. It is also said: the spirits of the martyrs terminate there.

﴿The Garden of Refuge﴾: the Garden to which the God-fearing go. Thus related al-Hasan. It is also said: the spirits of the martyrs take refuge in it.

And Ali and Ibn al-Zubayr and a group [of readers] recited: jannatu l-ma'wa (the Garden of Refuge), meaning: it covered it with its shadows and entered into it. It is reported from Aisha that she rejected this reading and said: "Whoever recites it that way, may God cover him [with a curse]." [Cf. the Arabic phrase: fa-ajannahu Allah.] "...what covered it" is an expression of magnification and amplification of what covered it. By this expression it is known that what covered it of creatures indicating the greatness and majesty of God are things that description cannot fathom and attribute cannot encompass. It has also been said: a vast multitude of angels covered it, worshipping God in its presence. And it is reported from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I saw on every leaf of it an angel standing, glorifying God." [Narrated by al-Tabari through the route of Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: it was said to him, "O Messenger of God, what did you see covering that tree?" and he mentioned it and completed it more than this. But Abd al-Rahman is weak, and this report is mu'dal (with two or more consecutive omissions in its chain).] And from him, peace be upon him: it was covered by a canopy (rafraf) of green birds. [I have not found it.] And from Ibn Mas'ud and others: it was covered by golden butterflies (farash min dhahab). [As for the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh narrated it through the route of Murrah from him with this wording and more. As for others, it was narrated by [blank space in the original].]

"His gaze did not swerve, nor did it transgress" (ma zaagha basaru Rasul Allah (ﷺ) wa ma taghaa): that is, he affirmed what he saw with certain and correct affirmation, without his gaze deviating from it or passing beyond it; or: he did not turn away from the wonders he was commanded to see and was enabled to see, and "nor did it transgress" means he did not go beyond what he was commanded to see.

"Indeed he saw of the signs of his Lord the greatest signs" (La-qad ra'a min ayati Rabbihi al-kubra): by God, he indeed saw of the signs of his Lord the signs that are greatest and most magnificent. [Mahmud said: "its meaning is: he indeed saw of the signs of his Lord the signs which..." etc. Ahmad says: It is possible that "the greatest" is an attribute of "signs of his Lord," not a direct object, and the seen object is omitted for magnifying and glorifying the matter, as if he said: "He indeed saw of the greatest signs of his Lord matters of great magnitude that description cannot encompass," and omission in such a case is more eloquent and awe-inspiring. This—and God knows best—is preferable to the first, because in it there is magnification of God's greatest signs, and that among them are what he saw and what he did not see. On the first interpretation, its implication would be that he saw all the greatest signs in totality and generality, and this is far-fetched, for no one can comprehensively know the totality of God's signs. If one says: it is a general term intended as a particular, then it returns to the interpretation we mentioned, and God knows best.]

That is, when he ascended to his Lord to the heavens, and was shown the wonders of the dominion (malakut).

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 53, verses 1–18 (part 1 of 2)**

Meccan [except verse 32, which is Medinan]. Its verses number 62, and it is said 61. [It was revealed after Surah al-Ikhlas.]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

*al-Najm* (the Star): the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), which is its dominant name. A poet said:

*When the Najm rises at night, the shepherd seeks a cloak.* [The Arabs say this about winter. About summer they say:

*When the Najm rises in the morning, the shepherd seeks a waterskin.*

*Al-Najm* is a name dominant over the Pleiades. It is said that it stays hidden for forty days in the year, its light concealed by the sun, and it appears at nightfall when winter begins and at dawn when summer begins. *Al-kisa'* (cloak) is a full garment. *Al-ghadiyya* is the diminutive of *ghadwa*, which is the early part of the day. *Al-shukiyya* is the diminutive of *shukwa*, which is a small, bare waterskin. In winter one seeks a thick cloak because of the great cold, and in summer one seeks a waterskin to drink from because of the great heat. The first is a metaphor for the arrival of cold, and the second for the arrival of heat.]

Or *al-najm* means the genus of stars. A poet said:

*Then she spent the night counting the stars in a restless state.* [They knew that I fulfilled my duty to its owner, so he set out on a hard she-camel, leading another beside her.

I hosted al-Kilabi, who sought hospitality, and your mother, when her camel was driven toward us.

So she spent the night counting the stars in a restless state, a swift one, whose ready contents were consumed by the eaters.

When we gave her the *'akis* (a mixture of broth and milk), she was filled, and her throat-veins swelled and trembled.

When she had satisfied a need from the vessel, she wanted from us a need we did not want.]

This is by al-Ra'i al-Numayri, of Banu Qutn ibn Rabi'a. Guests from Banu Kilab came to him while his camels were away, so he slaughtered for them one of their own riding camels. When morning came, his camels returned to him, so he gave the owner of the slaughtered camel its equivalent, plus an extra female camel in addition to it. Khanzar ibn Arqam of Banu Badr ibn Rabi'a blamed him for slaughtering it, and al-Ra'i replied with a poem containing this verse. *Al-'anas* is a hard she-camel. *Ummuka* is in apposition to *al-Kilabi*.

*Yuhda* is in the passive voice, meaning that she is driven onward with singing. *Al-qu'ud* (like *sabur*) is a young female camel, because a rider cannot sit on her back. Another version reads *idh yuhda ilayka* ("when she is driven toward you") instead of *ilaynā* ("toward us"). Perhaps this comes after the hospitality mentioned later, or it is a distortion.

*Fa-bata ummuka ta'udd al-najm*: she spent the night counting the forms of the stars, or counting the bubbles of broth in the bowl. He therefore uses *al-najm* as a metaphor in the form of explicit metaphor (*al-tasrihiyya*).

Or she counts the Pleiades, since *al-najm* is dominant over them, and they are seven stars whose shape is seen on winter nights. It is also said that *al-ʿadd* here means supposing, so that she spent the night supposing about it.

*Al-mustahira* means the one bewildered by being filled with broth. It is also transmitted as *mustajira*, because it draws people to eat from it. *Al-'akis* is broth mixed with fresh milk. *Tamallat* means became full. Another version reads *tamadhdhat* with a non-dotted *dhal*, meaning expanded from being satisfied. Another version reads it with a dotted letter, meaning knocked together and agitated. *Al-madhakhir* are the places of stores, meaning the stomach and intestines. Another version reads *khawasir*, meaning its sides. *Irtafad* means dripped, sprinkled, trembled, and fled. Another version reads *wazdada rashhan wariduha* (its veins increased in sweat).

The meaning is: she spent the night looking at the stars in a bowl abundant with broth and fat, whose fat quickly congealed in the hands of the eaters because of the winter cold. Until, when her belly was full and the veins of her neck were distended, and she had satisfied a need from the owner of the vessel (which is the broth and milk), she asked us for something we did not want or accept, because it was excessive. It is as if she intended the meaning of supplication, inclination, or relation, so he used *ila* after it. It is also permissible that *ila* means *min* (from), as we have explained at the end of the letter *ba'*.

*Yurid al-nujum idha hawa*: he means the stars when they set, or when they are scattered on the Day of Resurrection. Or *al-najm* is the star by which the devils are stoned, when it falls, or when it plunges down. Or *al-najm* is one of the stars of the Qur'an, which was sent down in portions over twenty years. *Idha hawa* means when it descended. Or *al-nabat* (plants): when it falls, meaning when it drops to the ground.

It is related from 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr that 'Utba ibn Abi Lahab, whose wife was the daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), intended to go out to Syria. He said, "I will go to Muhammad and harm him." He came to him and said, "O Muhammad, he disbelieves in the star when it falls, and in the one who drew near and then descended." Then he spat in the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), returned his daughter to him, and divorced her. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "O Allah, set upon him one of Your dogs." Abu Talib was present, and was stricken with grief [*fawajam lahā*, meaning his grief intensified. This is according to *al-Sihah*. (ʿA)]. He said, "How self-sufficient you would have been, O nephew, from this call!" 'Utba returned to his father and informed him. Then they went out toward Syria and camped at a station. A monk from the monastery overlooked them and said, "This is a land of predators." Abu Lahab said to his companions, "Help us, O company of Quraysh, this night, for I fear for my son because of Muhammad's supplication." So they gathered their camels and made them kneel around them, and they encircled 'Utba. A lion came, sniffing their faces, until it struck 'Utba and killed him. [Abu Nu'aym related it in *al-Dala'il* through Ibn Ishaq, from 'Uthman ibn 'Urwa, from his father, and mentioned something similar, except that he said, "The lion struck him with its tail one blow, and he died on the spot." Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* and al-Tabarani related it through Sa'id from Qatada at length, similar to this. But 'Anbasa said: al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi also related it in *al-Dala'il*, from the narration of Abu Nawfal ibn Abi 'Aqrab from his father, who said, "It was Lahab ibn Abi Lahab," and mentioned it briefly. Al-Bayhaqi said: this is what 'Abbas ibn al-Fadl al-Azraq said, but it is not strong. The people of the military expeditions say it was 'Utba or 'Utayba.]

Hassan said:

*Whoever returns this year to his family, the lion's prey will not return.* [*Lā yarfa'u al-Rahmanu maṣra'akum, wa lā yuwhinu quwwata al-ṣāri'*

*wa kāna fīhi lakum 'ibratun, al-sayyidu al-matbū'u wa al-tābi'*

*man yarji'u al-'ilma ilā ahlihi, fa-mā akīlu al-sab'i bi al-rāji'*

*man 'āda fa-al-layth lahu 'ā'id, a'ẓim bihi min khabar shā'i'*

These are by Hassan ibn Thabit. He related from 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr that 'Utba ibn Abi Lahab had the daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as his wife. He went to him and said, "He disbelieves in the star when it falls, and in the one who drew near and then descended." Then he spat in his face and divorced his daughter and went out to Syria. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "O Allah, set upon him one of Your dogs." Then, one night while they were guarding him on a journey, a lion came, sniffing their faces until it struck 'Utba and killed him. Hassan said this. The two verbs are in the jussive, governed by *lā* of supplication. *Yuwahhin* is with the intensive form, and its meaning is supplication against the slain and supplication for the slayer. *Al-maṣra'* means the one thrown down. *Al-'ibra* means consideration, or that by which one takes a lesson. *Al-tābi'* is in apposition to *al-sayyid*.

Meaning: whoever returns this year to his family, his return does not make another's return obligatory, because the one eaten by a predator does not return, so his family should not wish for his return, given its impossibility and the predator's habit. Then he said: whoever acts like 'Utba, the lion is his enemy. *A'ẓim bihi* is an exclamation form. *Min khabar* is a specification (*tamyīz*) accompanied by *min*. *Shā'i'* means widespread, spreading.]

﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾: the companion means Muhammad (ﷺ). The address is to Quraysh, and this is the answer to the oath. *Al-ḍalāl* is the opposite of guidance, and *al-ghayy* is the opposite of rightness. The meaning is: he is rightly guided and upright, and it is not as you claim when you attribute to him error and deviation. What he has brought you of the Qur'an is not speech issuing from his desire or opinion, but a revelation from Allah that is revealed to him. This verse is used as proof by those who do not consider *ijtihad* (independent reasoning) permissible for prophets. The answer is that when Allah permits them to exercise *ijtihad*, then *ijtihad* and what it rests upon is entirely revelation, not speech from desire.

﴿Taught him by one mighty in power﴾: an angel mighty in power. The genitive construction is not literal, because it is the attributive adjective (*al-ṣifa al-mushabbaha*) construed with its agent, and that is Jibril (peace be upon him). Among his strength: he uprooted the cities of the people of Lut from the black water and carried them on his wing, raised them to heaven, and then overturned them. He shouted a cry at Thamud and they became prostrate in their homes. His descent to the prophets and his ascent were swifter than the return of a glance [*fī awḥā min rij'at al-ṭarf*. (Note: *awḥā* means swifter than the wahy, which is speed; it may be read with madd or qasr. Also in *al-Sihah*: *nafaḥat al-nāqa* means she struck with her leg; *nafahahu bi-l-sayf* means he took it up. (ʿA)]. He saw Iblis speaking with 'Isa (peace be upon him) on some mountain of the holy land, so he struck him with his wing, a blow that cast him to the farthest mountain in India.

﴿Possessed of power﴾: possessed of soundness of intellect [*ḥaṣāfa fī 'aqlihi*, meaning firmness. This is according to *al-Sihah*. (ʿA)] and judgment, and firmness in his religion.

﴿Then he stood﴾: he stood upright in his true form, not in the form he used to take whenever he descended with revelation. He used to descend in the form of Dihya. That is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) loved to see him in the form in which he was created, so he appeared to him on the highest horizon, which is the horizon of the sun, and filled the horizon. [I have not found it in this form. In the two *Sahihs*, from the narration of Masruq from 'A'isha: "I was the first to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said, 'It is only Jibril. I did not see him in his form in which you saw him except these two times: I saw him descending from heaven, filling the expanse between heaven and earth with the greatness of his form.'" In al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Hibban: "But he saw Jibril; he did not see him in his form except twice: once at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, and once at Ajyad. He had six hundred wings, and he had filled the horizon."]

It is said: no prophet saw him in his true form except Muhammad (ﷺ), twice: once on earth and once in heaven. [I have not found this as stated. As for mentioning the two times, it was mentioned in the previous report.]

﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾: he approached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and was suspended in the air above him. From this comes *tadallat al-thamara* (the fruit hung down), and *dallā rijlayhi min al-sarīr* (he let his legs hang down from the bed).

*Al-dawālī* are the hanging fruits. A poet said:

*He hung down over them between a rope and a cord, hanging like the bucket of a drawing man, shaking.* [This line is attributed to Abu Dhu'ayb, the second half being: "with a bare mare like a leather mat, whose rider stumbles." *Al-sabb*, with a kasra, is a rope, a headband, or a turban. *Al-khayṭa* is likewise, meaning a peg or the like, in the dialect of Hudhayl. *Al-mā'iḥ* is the one who fills the bucket from the bottom of the well. *Al-māʾiḥ* (with a *ta'*) is the one who draws water. The poet describes the one who gathers honey as hanging over the bees or the honey, because it is also feminine. That is, he descended holding onto a rope fastened to a peg, like the bucket of an energetic filler. *Al-jardā'* is a mare with little hair. *Al-wakf* is a leather mat. *Kabā al-jawād yakbū* means it fell on its face. *Ghurāb al-dābba* is the upper part of its back, meaning that its back seems to slope because of the speed of its gait.]

It is said: he is like the *qarlā* [the kite? (a bird)]: if he sees good, he descends, and if he does not see it, he turns away.

*Qāba qawsayn*: the measure of two Arab bows. *Al-qāb*, *al-qayb*, *al-qād*, *al-qayd*, and *al-qays* all mean measure. Zayd ibn 'Ali read *qād*, and *qīd* and *qadr* are also read. Measurement has been given by the bow, the spear, the whip, the forearm, the arm's span, the stride, the handspan, the span of the fingers, and the finger. From this is the saying: "No prayer until the sun has risen to the measure of two spears." [Al-Hakim related it from the report of 'Amr ibn 'Abasa in a long hadith; Ishaq and al-Daraqutni related it from the report of Ka'b ibn Murra similarly, in a hadith; al-Tabarani related it from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf in brief.] In the hadith: "The space of the bow of one of you in Paradise, and the place of his whip, is better than the world and what is in it." [Al-Bukhari related it through Humayd from Anas, more complete than this.] *Al-qadd* is the whip.

It is said: there is a short distance between them. A poet said:

*And you have made me from Huzayma a finger's breadth.* [*Fa-adraka ibqā' al-'arāwa zal'ahā, wa qad ja'altanī min Huzayma iṣba'an*

This is by al-Kalhiyya, and it is a nickname of 'Abd Allah ibn Hubayra. It is also said to be Jarir ibn Hubayra, or Hubayra ibn 'Abd Manaf. It is also said to be by al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur, or Ru'ba, but this is nothing. *Al-ibqā'* is what the mare retains of her energy to spend near the reaching of the goal. *Al-'arāwa* is like *jarāda*; it is also said that with a kasra it is the name of his mare. *Al-zal'* (with a fatha) is a limp in gait from pain in the leg. Meaning: the limp overtook what the mare had retained, so she could not spend it, while she had made me close to my enemy Huzayma (with an unpointed *ha*, then a pointed *kasra*), a man who had raided the poet's camels and then been pursued by him. It is also said that it is his tribe, but this is not so. Another version reads *fa-adraka irqāl al-'arāwa*. *Al-irqāl* is hastening in movement, meaning that the limp nullified her speed. We must interpret his words "you made me a finger", meaning: you made me one whose distance is a finger's breadth, or you made my distance the measure of a finger.]

If you say: how is the measure in His words *fa-kāna qāba qawsayn*? I say: the measure is "the distance of his nearness was like the measure of two bows." [Mahmud said: "Its measure: the distance of his nearness was like the measure of two bows," to the end. Ahmad said: Some of them have said it is a metaphor for a covenant to adhere to obedience, because when two allies in Arab custom pledge themselves to loyalty and purity, they press together and their two bows are joined. Ahmad said: in this there is an inclination toward His words *aw adnā*.]

So these added terms are omitted, as Abu 'Ali said in his line:

*And you have made me from Huzayma a finger's breadth.*

That is: one with the measure of the distance of a finger's breadth. *Aw adnā*: that is, according to your estimate, like His words *aw yazīdūn* (or they increase). *Ilā 'abdihi*: to His servant, that is, to the servant of Allah, though no mention of His name has preceded, because there is no ambiguity, like His words *'alā ẓahrihā* (upon its back).

*Mā awḥā*: a glorification of the revelation that was revealed. [Mahmud said: "This is a glorification of the revelation that Allah revealed to him." Ahmad said: the glorification is because of what it contains of vagueness, as if it were too great to be encompassed by explanation. It is like His words *idh yaghshā al-sidrata mā yaghshā* and His words *fa-ghashiyahum min al-yammi mā ghashiyahum*.]

Its meaning: it was said that he was revealed: "Paradise is forbidden to the prophets until you enter it, and to the nations until your nation enters it."

﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾: the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not deny what his eyes saw of the form of Jibril (peace be upon him). That is, his heart did not say, when he saw it: "I do not recognize you," for had it said that, it would have been lying, because he recognized him. The meaning is that he saw him with his eyes and recognized him with his heart, and he did not doubt that what he saw was true. It is also read *mā kadhaba*, meaning that he confirmed it, and did not doubt that it was Jibril (peace be upon him) in his form.

﴿Will you dispute with him what he saw?﴾: from *al-mirā'*, which is contention and argument. Its derivation is from *maraya al-nāqa* (he milked the she-camel), as if each of the two disputants milks what is with his companion. It is also read *afa-tamrūnahu*, meaning: will you overcome him in disputation, from *mārayatuhu fa-maraytuhu*. Because of the meaning of victory in it, it is construed with *'alā*, as you say "I overcame him in such-and-such." It is also said that *afa-tamrūnahu* means: will you deny him. They have recited:

*If you revile a brother of truth and nobility, you have indeed milked a brother who was not one to be milked by you.* [He says to his companion: if you blame a brother of truth and nobility, meaning himself. It is said: *maraya al-nāqa*, meaning he milked her. From this comes *al-mirā'*, as if each of the two disputants milks what is with his companion. From it: "you have indeed contended with a brother of truth," meaning you overcame him in dispute and drew out what was with him, because whoever milks a she-camel leaves her udder dry, or you denied his right as if you had taken it from him, or you caused what was with him to come out, so he blames you as you blamed him. *Mā kāna yumrīka*, meaning: what he did not do to you like that.]

They also said: it is said *mariyatuhu ḥaqqahu* when you deny it. Its construction with *'alā* is valid only according to the doctrine of implication (*taḍmīn*).

﴿Another descent﴾: a second time of descending. The word *nazla* is put in the accusative in the manner of the adverb of time, which is "once", because the form *fa'la* is a noun for the single occurrence of the verb, so it has its ruling. That is: Jibril (peace be upon him) descended upon him a second descent in his own form, and he saw him in it. That was on the night of the Ascension (*mi'rāj*).

It is said about the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (*sidrat al-muntahā*): it is a jujube tree in the seventh heaven, to the right of the Throne. Its fruit is like the jars of Hajar, and its leaves are like the ears of elephants. From its root flow the rivers which Allah mentioned in His Book. A rider walks in its shade for seventy years without crossing it.

*Al-muntahā* means the place of ending, or the ending itself, as if it were at the furthest limit and end of Paradise. It is also said: no one has passed beyond it, and to it the knowledge of the angels and others ends, and no one knows what is beyond it. It is also said: the spirits of the martyrs terminate there.

﴿The Garden of Refuge﴾: the Garden to which the God-fearing go. Thus related al-Hasan. It is also said: the spirits of the martyrs take refuge in it.

And Ali and Ibn al-Zubayr and a group [of readers] recited: jannatu l-ma'wa (the Garden of Refuge), meaning: it covered it with its shadows and entered into it. It is reported from Aisha that she rejected this reading and said: "Whoever recites it that way, may God cover him [with a curse]." [Cf. the Arabic phrase: fa-ajannahu Allah.] "...what covered it" is an expression of magnification and amplification of what covered it. By this expression it is known that what covered it of creatures indicating the greatness and majesty of God are things that description cannot fathom and attribute cannot encompass. It has also been said: a vast multitude of angels covered it, worshipping God in its presence. And it is reported from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I saw on every leaf of it an angel standing, glorifying God." [Narrated by al-Tabari through the route of Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: it was said to him, "O Messenger of God, what did you see covering that tree?" and he mentioned it and completed it more than this. But Abd al-Rahman is weak, and this report is mu'dal (with two or more consecutive omissions in its chain).] And from him, peace be upon him: it was covered by a canopy (rafraf) of green birds. [I have not found it.] And from Ibn Mas'ud and others: it was covered by golden butterflies (farash min dhahab). [As for the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh narrated it through the route of Murrah from him with this wording and more. As for others, it was narrated by [blank space in the original].]

"His gaze did not swerve, nor did it transgress" (ma zaagha basaru Rasul Allah (ﷺ) wa ma taghaa): that is, he affirmed what he saw with certain and correct affirmation, without his gaze deviating from it or passing beyond it; or: he did not turn away from the wonders he was commanded to see and was enabled to see, and "nor did it transgress" means he did not go beyond what he was commanded to see.

"Indeed he saw of the signs of his Lord the greatest signs" (La-qad ra'a min ayati Rabbihi al-kubra): by God, he indeed saw of the signs of his Lord the signs that are greatest and most magnificent. [Mahmud said: "its meaning is: he indeed saw of the signs of his Lord the signs which..." etc. Ahmad says: It is possible that "the greatest" is an attribute of "signs of his Lord," not a direct object, and the seen object is omitted for magnifying and glorifying the matter, as if he said: "He indeed saw of the greatest signs of his Lord matters of great magnitude that description cannot encompass," and omission in such a case is more eloquent and awe-inspiring. This—and God knows best—is preferable to the first, because in it there is magnification of God's greatest signs, and that among them are what he saw and what he did not see. On the first interpretation, its implication would be that he saw all the greatest signs in totality and generality, and this is far-fetched, for no one can comprehensively know the totality of God's signs. If one says: it is a general term intended as a particular, then it returns to the interpretation we mentioned, and God knows best.]

That is, when he ascended to his Lord to the heavens, and was shown the wonders of the dominion (malakut).

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 53, verses 1–18 (part 1 of 2)**

Meccan [except verse 32, which is Medinan]. Its verses number 62, and it is said 61. [It was revealed after Surah al-Ikhlas.]

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

*al-Najm* (the Star): the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), which is its dominant name. A poet said:

*When the Najm rises at night, the shepherd seeks a cloak.* [The Arabs say this about winter. About summer they say:

*When the Najm rises in the morning, the shepherd seeks a waterskin.*

*Al-Najm* is a name dominant over the Pleiades. It is said that it stays hidden for forty days in the year, its light concealed by the sun, and it appears at nightfall when winter begins and at dawn when summer begins. *Al-kisa'* (cloak) is a full garment. *Al-ghadiyya* is the diminutive of *ghadwa*, which is the early part of the day. *Al-shukiyya* is the diminutive of *shukwa*, which is a small, bare waterskin. In winter one seeks a thick cloak because of the great cold, and in summer one seeks a waterskin to drink from because of the great heat. The first is a metaphor for the arrival of cold, and the second for the arrival of heat.]

Or *al-najm* means the genus of stars. A poet said:

*Then she spent the night counting the stars in a restless state.* [They knew that I fulfilled my duty to its owner, so he set out on a hard she-camel, leading another beside her.

I hosted al-Kilabi, who sought hospitality, and your mother, when her camel was driven toward us.

So she spent the night counting the stars in a restless state, a swift one, whose ready contents were consumed by the eaters.

When we gave her the *'akis* (a mixture of broth and milk), she was filled, and her throat-veins swelled and trembled.

When she had satisfied a need from the vessel, she wanted from us a need we did not want.]

This is by al-Ra'i al-Numayri, of Banu Qutn ibn Rabi'a. Guests from Banu Kilab came to him while his camels were away, so he slaughtered for them one of their own riding camels. When morning came, his camels returned to him, so he gave the owner of the slaughtered camel its equivalent, plus an extra female camel in addition to it. Khanzar ibn Arqam of Banu Badr ibn Rabi'a blamed him for slaughtering it, and al-Ra'i replied with a poem containing this verse. *Al-'anas* is a hard she-camel. *Ummuka* is in apposition to *al-Kilabi*.

*Yuhda* is in the passive voice, meaning that she is driven onward with singing. *Al-qu'ud* (like *sabur*) is a young female camel, because a rider cannot sit on her back. Another version reads *idh yuhda ilayka* ("when she is driven toward you") instead of *ilaynā* ("toward us"). Perhaps this comes after the hospitality mentioned later, or it is a distortion.

*Fa-bata ummuka ta'udd al-najm*: she spent the night counting the forms of the stars, or counting the bubbles of broth in the bowl. He therefore uses *al-najm* as a metaphor in the form of explicit metaphor (*al-tasrihiyya*).

Or she counts the Pleiades, since *al-najm* is dominant over them, and they are seven stars whose shape is seen on winter nights. It is also said that *al-ʿadd* here means supposing, so that she spent the night supposing about it.

*Al-mustahira* means the one bewildered by being filled with broth. It is also transmitted as *mustajira*, because it draws people to eat from it. *Al-'akis* is broth mixed with fresh milk. *Tamallat* means became full. Another version reads *tamadhdhat* with a non-dotted *dhal*, meaning expanded from being satisfied. Another version reads it with a dotted letter, meaning knocked together and agitated. *Al-madhakhir* are the places of stores, meaning the stomach and intestines. Another version reads *khawasir*, meaning its sides. *Irtafad* means dripped, sprinkled, trembled, and fled. Another version reads *wazdada rashhan wariduha* (its veins increased in sweat).

The meaning is: she spent the night looking at the stars in a bowl abundant with broth and fat, whose fat quickly congealed in the hands of the eaters because of the winter cold. Until, when her belly was full and the veins of her neck were distended, and she had satisfied a need from the owner of the vessel (which is the broth and milk), she asked us for something we did not want or accept, because it was excessive. It is as if she intended the meaning of supplication, inclination, or relation, so he used *ila* after it. It is also permissible that *ila* means *min* (from), as we have explained at the end of the letter *ba'*.

*Yurid al-nujum idha hawa*: he means the stars when they set, or when they are scattered on the Day of Resurrection. Or *al-najm* is the star by which the devils are stoned, when it falls, or when it plunges down. Or *al-najm* is one of the stars of the Qur'an, which was sent down in portions over twenty years. *Idha hawa* means when it descended. Or *al-nabat* (plants): when it falls, meaning when it drops to the ground.

It is related from 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr that 'Utba ibn Abi Lahab, whose wife was the daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), intended to go out to Syria. He said, "I will go to Muhammad and harm him." He came to him and said, "O Muhammad, he disbelieves in the star when it falls, and in the one who drew near and then descended." Then he spat in the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), returned his daughter to him, and divorced her. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "O Allah, set upon him one of Your dogs." Abu Talib was present, and was stricken with grief [*fawajam lahā*, meaning his grief intensified. This is according to *al-Sihah*. (ʿA)]. He said, "How self-sufficient you would have been, O nephew, from this call!" 'Utba returned to his father and informed him. Then they went out toward Syria and camped at a station. A monk from the monastery overlooked them and said, "This is a land of predators." Abu Lahab said to his companions, "Help us, O company of Quraysh, this night, for I fear for my son because of Muhammad's supplication." So they gathered their camels and made them kneel around them, and they encircled 'Utba. A lion came, sniffing their faces, until it struck 'Utba and killed him. [Abu Nu'aym related it in *al-Dala'il* through Ibn Ishaq, from 'Uthman ibn 'Urwa, from his father, and mentioned something similar, except that he said, "The lion struck him with its tail one blow, and he died on the spot." Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* and al-Tabarani related it through Sa'id from Qatada at length, similar to this. But 'Anbasa said: al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi also related it in *al-Dala'il*, from the narration of Abu Nawfal ibn Abi 'Aqrab from his father, who said, "It was Lahab ibn Abi Lahab," and mentioned it briefly. Al-Bayhaqi said: this is what 'Abbas ibn al-Fadl al-Azraq said, but it is not strong. The people of the military expeditions say it was 'Utba or 'Utayba.]

Hassan said:

*Whoever returns this year to his family, the lion's prey will not return.* [*Lā yarfa'u al-Rahmanu maṣra'akum, wa lā yuwhinu quwwata al-ṣāri'*

*wa kāna fīhi lakum 'ibratun, al-sayyidu al-matbū'u wa al-tābi'*

*man yarji'u al-'ilma ilā ahlihi, fa-mā akīlu al-sab'i bi al-rāji'*

*man 'āda fa-al-layth lahu 'ā'id, a'ẓim bihi min khabar shā'i'*

These are by Hassan ibn Thabit. He related from 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr that 'Utba ibn Abi Lahab had the daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as his wife. He went to him and said, "He disbelieves in the star when it falls, and in the one who drew near and then descended." Then he spat in his face and divorced his daughter and went out to Syria. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "O Allah, set upon him one of Your dogs." Then, one night while they were guarding him on a journey, a lion came, sniffing their faces until it struck 'Utba and killed him. Hassan said this. The two verbs are in the jussive, governed by *lā* of supplication. *Yuwahhin* is with the intensive form, and its meaning is supplication against the slain and supplication for the slayer. *Al-maṣra'* means the one thrown down. *Al-'ibra* means consideration, or that by which one takes a lesson. *Al-tābi'* is in apposition to *al-sayyid*.

Meaning: whoever returns this year to his family, his return does not make another's return obligatory, because the one eaten by a predator does not return, so his family should not wish for his return, given its impossibility and the predator's habit. Then he said: whoever acts like 'Utba, the lion is his enemy. *A'ẓim bihi* is an exclamation form. *Min khabar* is a specification (*tamyīz*) accompanied by *min*. *Shā'i'* means widespread, spreading.]

﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾: the companion means Muhammad (ﷺ). The address is to Quraysh, and this is the answer to the oath. *Al-ḍalāl* is the opposite of guidance, and *al-ghayy* is the opposite of rightness. The meaning is: he is rightly guided and upright, and it is not as you claim when you attribute to him error and deviation. What he has brought you of the Qur'an is not speech issuing from his desire or opinion, but a revelation from Allah that is revealed to him. This verse is used as proof by those who do not consider *ijtihad* (independent reasoning) permissible for prophets. The answer is that when Allah permits them to exercise *ijtihad*, then *ijtihad* and what it rests upon is entirely revelation, not speech from desire.

﴿Taught him by one mighty in power﴾: an angel mighty in power. The genitive construction is not literal, because it is the attributive adjective (*al-ṣifa al-mushabbaha*) construed with its agent, and that is Jibril (peace be upon him). Among his strength: he uprooted the cities of the people of Lut from the black water and carried them on his wing, raised them to heaven, and then overturned them. He shouted a cry at Thamud and they became prostrate in their homes. His descent to the prophets and his ascent were swifter than the return of a glance [*fī awḥā min rij'at al-ṭarf*. (Note: *awḥā* means swifter than the wahy, which is speed; it may be read with madd or qasr. Also in *al-Sihah*: *nafaḥat al-nāqa* means she struck with her leg; *nafahahu bi-l-sayf* means he took it up. (ʿA)]. He saw Iblis speaking with 'Isa (peace be upon him) on some mountain of the holy land, so he struck him with his wing, a blow that cast him to the farthest mountain in India.

﴿Possessed of power﴾: possessed of soundness of intellect [*ḥaṣāfa fī 'aqlihi*, meaning firmness. This is according to *al-Sihah*. (ʿA)] and judgment, and firmness in his religion.

﴿Then he stood﴾: he stood upright in his true form, not in the form he used to take whenever he descended with revelation. He used to descend in the form of Dihya. That is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) loved to see him in the form in which he was created, so he appeared to him on the highest horizon, which is the horizon of the sun, and filled the horizon. [I have not found it in this form. In the two *Sahihs*, from the narration of Masruq from 'A'isha: "I was the first to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said, 'It is only Jibril. I did not see him in his form in which you saw him except these two times: I saw him descending from heaven, filling the expanse between heaven and earth with the greatness of his form.'" In al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Hibban: "But he saw Jibril; he did not see him in his form except twice: once at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, and once at Ajyad. He had six hundred wings, and he had filled the horizon."]

It is said: no prophet saw him in his true form except Muhammad (ﷺ), twice: once on earth and once in heaven. [I have not found this as stated. As for mentioning the two times, it was mentioned in the previous report.]

﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾: he approached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and was suspended in the air above him. From this comes *tadallat al-thamara* (the fruit hung down), and *dallā rijlayhi min al-sarīr* (he let his legs hang down from the bed).

*Al-dawālī* are the hanging fruits. A poet said:

*He hung down over them between a rope and a cord, hanging like the bucket of a drawing man, shaking.* [This line is attributed to Abu Dhu'ayb, the second half being: "with a bare mare like a leather mat, whose rider stumbles." *Al-sabb*, with a kasra, is a rope, a headband, or a turban. *Al-khayṭa* is likewise, meaning a peg or the like, in the dialect of Hudhayl. *Al-mā'iḥ* is the one who fills the bucket from the bottom of the well. *Al-māʾiḥ* (with a *ta'*) is the one who draws water. The poet describes the one who gathers honey as hanging over the bees or the honey, because it is also feminine. That is, he descended holding onto a rope fastened to a peg, like the bucket of an energetic filler. *Al-jardā'* is a mare with little hair. *Al-wakf* is a leather mat. *Kabā al-jawād yakbū* means it fell on its face. *Ghurāb al-dābba* is the upper part of its back, meaning that its back seems to slope because of the speed of its gait.]

It is said: he is like the *qarlā* [the kite? (a bird)]: if he sees good, he descends, and if he does not see it, he turns away.

*Qāba qawsayn*: the measure of two Arab bows. *Al-qāb*, *al-qayb*, *al-qād*, *al-qayd*, and *al-qays* all mean measure. Zayd ibn 'Ali read *qād*, and *qīd* and *qadr* are also read. Measurement has been given by the bow, the spear, the whip, the forearm, the arm's span, the stride, the handspan, the span of the fingers, and the finger. From this is the saying: "No prayer until the sun has risen to the measure of two spears." [Al-Hakim related it from the report of 'Amr ibn 'Abasa in a long hadith; Ishaq and al-Daraqutni related it from the report of Ka'b ibn Murra similarly, in a hadith; al-Tabarani related it from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf in brief.] In the hadith: "The space of the bow of one of you in Paradise, and the place of his whip, is better than the world and what is in it." [Al-Bukhari related it through Humayd from Anas, more complete than this.] *Al-qadd* is the whip.

It is said: there is a short distance between them. A poet said:

*And you have made me from Huzayma a finger's breadth.* [*Fa-adraka ibqā' al-'arāwa zal'ahā, wa qad ja'altanī min Huzayma iṣba'an*

This is by al-Kalhiyya, and it is a nickname of 'Abd Allah ibn Hubayra. It is also said to be Jarir ibn Hubayra, or Hubayra ibn 'Abd Manaf. It is also said to be by al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur, or Ru'ba, but this is nothing. *Al-ibqā'* is what the mare retains of her energy to spend near the reaching of the goal. *Al-'arāwa* is like *jarāda*; it is also said that with a kasra it is the name of his mare. *Al-zal'* (with a fatha) is a limp in gait from pain in the leg. Meaning: the limp overtook what the mare had retained, so she could not spend it, while she had made me close to my enemy Huzayma (with an unpointed *ha*, then a pointed *kasra*), a man who had raided the poet's camels and then been pursued by him. It is also said that it is his tribe, but this is not so. Another version reads *fa-adraka irqāl al-'arāwa*. *Al-irqāl* is hastening in movement, meaning that the limp nullified her speed. We must interpret his words "you made me a finger", meaning: you made me one whose distance is a finger's breadth, or you made my distance the measure of a finger.]

If you say: how is the measure in His words *fa-kāna qāba qawsayn*? I say: the measure is "the distance of his nearness was like the measure of two bows." [Mahmud said: "Its measure: the distance of his nearness was like the measure of two bows," to the end. Ahmad said: Some of them have said it is a metaphor for a covenant to adhere to obedience, because when two allies in Arab custom pledge themselves to loyalty and purity, they press together and their two bows are joined. Ahmad said: in this there is an inclination toward His words *aw adnā*.]

So these added terms are omitted, as Abu 'Ali said in his line:

*And you have made me from Huzayma a finger's breadth.*

That is: one with the measure of the distance of a finger's breadth. *Aw adnā*: that is, according to your estimate, like His words *aw yazīdūn* (or they increase). *Ilā 'abdihi*: to His servant, that is, to the servant of Allah, though no mention of His name has preceded, because there is no ambiguity, like His words *'alā ẓahrihā* (upon its back).

*Mā awḥā*: a glorification of the revelation that was revealed. [Mahmud said: "This is a glorification of the revelation that Allah revealed to him." Ahmad said: the glorification is because of what it contains of vagueness, as if it were too great to be encompassed by explanation. It is like His words *idh yaghshā al-sidrata mā yaghshā* and His words *fa-ghashiyahum min al-yammi mā ghashiyahum*.]

Its meaning: it was said that he was revealed: "Paradise is forbidden to the prophets until you enter it, and to the nations until your nation enters it."

﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾: the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not deny what his eyes saw of the form of Jibril (peace be upon him). That is, his heart did not say, when he saw it: "I do not recognize you," for had it said that, it would have been lying, because he recognized him. The meaning is that he saw him with his eyes and recognized him with his heart, and he did not doubt that what he saw was true. It is also read *mā kadhaba*, meaning that he confirmed it, and did not doubt that it was Jibril (peace be upon him) in his form.

﴿Will you dispute with him what he saw?﴾: from *al-mirā'*, which is contention and argument. Its derivation is from *maraya al-nāqa* (he milked the she-camel), as if each of the two disputants milks what is with his companion. It is also read *afa-tamrūnahu*, meaning: will you overcome him in disputation, from *mārayatuhu fa-maraytuhu*. Because of the meaning of victory in it, it is construed with *'alā*, as you say "I overcame him in such-and-such." It is also said that *afa-tamrūnahu* means: will you deny him. They have recited:

*If you revile a brother of truth and nobility, you have indeed milked a brother who was not one to be milked by you.* [He says to his companion: if you blame a brother of truth and nobility, meaning himself. It is said: *maraya al-nāqa*, meaning he milked her. From this comes *al-mirā'*, as if each of the two disputants milks what is with his companion. From it: "you have indeed contended with a brother of truth," meaning you overcame him in dispute and drew out what was with him, because whoever milks a she-camel leaves her udder dry, or you denied his right as if you had taken it from him, or you caused what was with him to come out, so he blames you as you blamed him. *Mā kāna yumrīka*, meaning: what he did not do to you like that.]

They also said: it is said *mariyatuhu ḥaqqahu* when you deny it. Its construction with *'alā* is valid only according to the doctrine of implication (*taḍmīn*).

﴿Another descent﴾: a second time of descending. The word *nazla* is put in the accusative in the manner of the adverb of time, which is "once", because the form *fa'la* is a noun for the single occurrence of the verb, so it has its ruling. That is: Jibril (peace be upon him) descended upon him a second descent in his own form, and he saw him in it. That was on the night of the Ascension (*mi'rāj*).

It is said about the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (*sidrat al-muntahā*): it is a jujube tree in the seventh heaven, to the right of the Throne. Its fruit is like the jars of Hajar, and its leaves are like the ears of elephants. From its root flow the rivers which Allah mentioned in His Book. A rider walks in its shade for seventy years without crossing it.

*Al-muntahā* means the place of ending, or the ending itself, as if it were at the furthest limit and end of Paradise. It is also said: no one has passed beyond it, and to it the knowledge of the angels and others ends, and no one knows what is beyond it. It is also said: the spirits of the martyrs terminate there.

﴿The Garden of Refuge﴾: the Garden to which the God-fearing go. Thus related al-Hasan. It is also said: the spirits of the martyrs take refuge in it.
