It is also transmitted as *mustajira*, because it draws people to eat from it. *Al-'akis* is broth mixed with fresh milk. *Tamallat* means became full. Another version reads *tamadhdhat* with a non-dotted *dhal*, meaning expanded from being satisfied. Another version reads it with a dotted letter, meaning knocked together and agitated. *Al-madhakhir* are the places of stores, meaning the stomach and intestines. Another version reads *khawasir*, meaning its sides. *Irtafad* means dripped, sprinkled, trembled, and fled. Another version reads *wazdada rashhan wariduha* (its veins increased in sweat).

The meaning is: she spent the night looking at the stars in a bowl abundant with broth and fat, whose fat quickly congealed in the hands of the eaters because of the winter cold. Until, when her belly was full and the veins of her neck were distended, and she had satisfied a need from the owner of the vessel (which is the broth and milk), she asked us for something we did not want or accept, because it was excessive. It is as if she intended the meaning of supplication, inclination, or relation, so he used *ila* after it. It is also permissible that *ila* means *min* (from), as we have explained at the end of the letter *ba'*.

*Yurid al-nujum idha hawa*: he means the stars when they set, or when they are scattered on the Day of Resurrection. Or *al-najm* is the star by which the devils are stoned, when it falls, or when it plunges down. Or *al-najm* is one of the stars of the Qur'an, which was sent down in portions over twenty years. *Idha hawa* means when it descended. Or *al-nabat* (plants): when it falls, meaning when it drops to the ground.

It is related from 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr that 'Utba ibn Abi Lahab, whose wife was the daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), intended to go out to Syria. He said, "I will go to Muhammad and harm him." He came to him and said, "O Muhammad, he disbelieves in the star when it falls, and in the one who drew near and then descended." Then he spat in the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), returned his daughter to him, and divorced her. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "O Allah, set upon him one of Your dogs." Abu Talib was present, and was stricken with grief [*fawajam lahā*, meaning his grief intensified. This is according to *al-Sihah*. (ʿA)]. He said, "How self-sufficient you would have been, O nephew, from this call!" 'Utba returned to his father and informed him. Then they went out toward Syria and camped at a station. A monk from the monastery overlooked them and said, "This is a land of predators." Abu Lahab said to his companions, "Help us, O company of Quraysh, this night, for I fear for my son because of Muhammad's supplication." So they gathered their camels and made them kneel around them, and they encircled 'Utba. A lion came, sniffing their faces, until it struck 'Utba and killed him. [Abu Nu'aym related it in *al-Dala'il* through Ibn Ishaq, from 'Uthman ibn 'Urwa, from his father, and mentioned something similar, except that he said, "The lion struck him with its tail one blow, and he died on the spot." Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* and al-Tabarani related it through Sa'id from Qatada at length, similar to this. But 'Anbasa said: al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi also related it in *al-Dala'il*, from the narration of Abu Nawfal ibn Abi 'Aqrab from his father, who said, "It was Lahab ibn Abi Lahab," and mentioned it briefly. Al-Bayhaqi said: this is what 'Abbas ibn al-Fadl al-Azraq said, but it is not strong. The people of the military expeditions say it was 'Utba or 'Utayba.]

Hassan said:

*Whoever returns this year to his family, the lion's prey will not return.* [*Lā yarfa'u al-Rahmanu maṣra'akum, wa lā yuwhinu quwwata al-ṣāri'*

*wa kāna fīhi lakum 'ibratun, al-sayyidu al-matbū'u wa al-tābi'*

*man yarji'u al-'ilma ilā ahlihi, fa-mā akīlu al-sab'i bi al-rāji'*

*man 'āda fa-al-layth lahu 'ā'id, a'ẓim bihi min khabar shā'i'*

These are by Hassan ibn Thabit. He related from 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr that 'Utba ibn Abi Lahab had the daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as his wife. He went to him and said, "He disbelieves in the star when it falls, and in the one who drew near and then descended." Then he spat in his face and divorced his daughter and went out to Syria. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, "O Allah, set upon him one of Your dogs." Then, one night while they were guarding him on a journey, a lion came, sniffing their faces until it struck 'Utba and killed him. Hassan said this. The two verbs are in the jussive, governed by *lā* of supplication. *Yuwahhin* is with the intensive form, and its meaning is supplication against the slain and supplication for the slayer. *Al-maṣra'* means the one thrown down. *Al-'ibra* means consideration, or that by which one takes a lesson. *Al-tābi'* is in apposition to *al-sayyid*.

Meaning: whoever returns this year to his family, his return does not make another's return obligatory, because the one eaten by a predator does not return, so his family should not wish for his return, given its impossibility and the predator's habit. Then he said: whoever acts like 'Utba, the lion is his enemy. *A'ẓim bihi* is an exclamation form. *Min khabar* is a specification (*tamyīz*) accompanied by *min*. *Shā'i'* means widespread, spreading.]

﴿Your companion has not strayed, nor has he erred﴾: the companion means Muhammad (ﷺ). The address is to Quraysh, and this is the answer to the oath. *Al-ḍalāl* is the opposite of guidance, and *al-ghayy* is the opposite of rightness. The meaning is: he is rightly guided and upright, and it is not as you claim when you attribute to him error and deviation. What he has brought you of the Qur'an is not speech issuing from his desire or opinion, but a revelation from Allah that is revealed to him. This verse is used as proof by those who do not consider *ijtihad* (independent reasoning) permissible for prophets. The answer is that when Allah permits them to exercise *ijtihad*, then *ijtihad* and what it rests upon is entirely revelation, not speech from desire.

﴿Taught him by one mighty in power﴾: an angel mighty in power. The genitive construction is not literal, because it is the attributive adjective (*al-ṣifa al-mushabbaha*) construed with its agent, and that is Jibril (peace be upon him). Among his strength: he uprooted the cities of the people of Lut from the black water and carried them on his wing, raised them to heaven, and then overturned them. He shouted a cry at Thamud and they became prostrate in their homes. His descent to the prophets and his ascent were swifter than the return of a glance [*fī awḥā min rij'at al-ṭarf*. (Note: *awḥā* means swifter than the wahy, which is speed; it may be read with madd or qasr. Also in *al-Sihah*: *nafaḥat al-nāqa* means she struck with her leg; *nafahahu bi-l-sayf* means he took it up. (ʿA)]. He saw Iblis speaking with 'Isa (peace be upon him) on some mountain of the holy land, so he struck him with his wing, a blow that cast him to the farthest mountain in India.

﴿Possessed of power﴾: possessed of soundness of intellect [*ḥaṣāfa fī 'aqlihi*, meaning firmness. This is according to *al-Sihah*. (ʿA)] and judgment, and firmness in his religion.

﴿Then he stood﴾: he stood upright in his true form, not in the form he used to take whenever he descended with revelation. He used to descend in the form of Dihya. That is because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) loved to see him in the form in which he was created, so he appeared to him on the highest horizon, which is the horizon of the sun, and filled the horizon. [I have not found it in this form. In the two *Sahihs*, from the narration of Masruq from 'A'isha: "I was the first to ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said, 'It is only Jibril. I did not see him in his form in which you saw him except these two times: I saw him descending from heaven, filling the expanse between heaven and earth with the greatness of his form.'" In al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Hibban: "But he saw Jibril; he did not see him in his form except twice: once at the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary, and once at Ajyad. He had six hundred wings, and he had filled the horizon."]

It is said: no prophet saw him in his true form except Muhammad (ﷺ), twice: once on earth and once in heaven. [I have not found this as stated. As for mentioning the two times, it was mentioned in the previous report.]

﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾: he approached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and was suspended in the air above him. From this comes *tadallat al-thamara* (the fruit hung down), and *dallā rijlayhi min al-sarīr* (he let his legs hang down from the bed).

*Al-dawālī* are the hanging fruits. A poet said:

*He hung down over them between a rope and a cord, hanging like the bucket of a drawing man, shaking.* [This line is attributed to Abu Dhu'ayb, the second half being: "with a bare mare like a leather mat, whose rider stumbles." *Al-sabb*, with a kasra, is a rope, a headband, or a turban. *Al-khayṭa* is likewise, meaning a peg or the like, in the dialect of Hudhayl. *Al-mā'iḥ* is the one who fills the bucket from the bottom of the well. *Al-māʾiḥ* (with a *ta'*) is the one who draws water. The poet describes the one who gathers honey as hanging over the bees or the honey, because it is also feminine. That is, he descended holding onto a rope fastened to a peg, like the bucket of an energetic filler. *Al-jardā'* is a mare with little hair. *Al-wakf* is a leather mat. *Kabā al-jawād yakbū* means it fell on its face. *Ghurāb al-dābba* is the upper part of its back, meaning that its back seems to slope because of the speed of its gait.]

It is said: he is like the *qarlā* [the kite? (a bird)]: if he sees good, he descends, and if he does not see it, he turns away.

*Qāba qawsayn*: the measure of two Arab bows. *Al-qāb*, *al-qayb*, *al-qād*, *al-qayd*, and *al-qays* all mean measure. Zayd ibn 'Ali read *qād*, and *qīd* and *qadr* are also read. Measurement has been given by the bow, the spear, the whip, the forearm, the arm's span, the stride, the handspan, the span of the fingers, and the finger. From this is the saying: "No prayer until the sun has risen to the measure of two spears." [Al-Hakim related it from the report of 'Amr ibn 'Abasa in a long hadith; Ishaq and al-Daraqutni related it from the report of Ka'b ibn Murra similarly, in a hadith; al-Tabarani related it from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf in brief.] In the hadith: "The space of the bow of one of you in Paradise, and the place of his whip, is better than the world and what is in it." [Al-Bukhari related it through Humayd from Anas, more complete than this.] *Al-qadd* is the whip.

It is said: there is a short distance between them. A poet said:

*And you have made me from Huzayma a finger's breadth.* [*Fa-adraka ibqā' al-'arāwa zal'ahā, wa qad ja'altanī min Huzayma iṣba'an*

This is by al-Kalhiyya, and it is a nickname of 'Abd Allah ibn Hubayra. It is also said to be Jarir ibn Hubayra, or Hubayra ibn 'Abd Manaf. It is also said to be by al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur, or Ru'ba, but this is nothing. *Al-ibqā'* is what the mare retains of her energy to spend near the reaching of the goal. *Al-'arāwa* is like *jarāda*; it is also said that with a kasra it is the name of his mare. *Al-zal'* (with a fatha) is a limp in gait from pain in the leg. Meaning: the limp overtook what the mare had retained, so she could not spend it, while she had made me close to my enemy Huzayma (with an unpointed *ha*, then a pointed *kasra*), a man who had raided the poet's camels and then been pursued by him. It is also said that it is his tribe, but this is not so. Another version reads *fa-adraka irqāl al-'arāwa*. *Al-irqāl* is hastening in movement, meaning that the limp nullified her speed. We must interpret his words "you made me a finger", meaning: you made me one whose distance is a finger's breadth, or you made my distance the measure of a finger.]

If you say: how is the measure in His words *fa-kāna qāba qawsayn*? I say: the measure is "the distance of his nearness was like the measure of two bows." [Mahmud said: "Its measure: the distance of his nearness was like the measure of two bows," to the end. Ahmad said: Some of them have said it is a metaphor for a covenant to adhere to obedience, because when two allies in Arab custom pledge themselves to loyalty and purity, they press together and their two bows are joined. Ahmad said: in this there is an inclination toward His words *aw adnā*.]

So these added terms are omitted, as Abu 'Ali said in his line:

*And you have made me from Huzayma a finger's breadth.*

That is: one with the measure of the distance of a finger's breadth. *Aw adnā*: that is, according to your estimate, like His words *aw yazīdūn* (or they increase). *Ilā 'abdihi*: to His servant, that is, to the servant of Allah, though no mention of His name has preceded, because there is no ambiguity, like His words *'alā ẓahrihā* (upon its back).

*Mā awḥā*: a glorification of the revelation that was revealed. [Mahmud said: "This is a glorification of the revelation that Allah revealed to him." Ahmad said: the glorification is because of what it contains of vagueness, as if it were too great to be encompassed by explanation. It is like His words *idh yaghshā al-sidrata mā yaghshā* and His words *fa-ghashiyahum min al-yammi mā ghashiyahum*.]

Its meaning: it was said that he was revealed: "Paradise is forbidden to the prophets until you enter it, and to the nations until your nation enters it."

﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾: the heart of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not deny what his eyes saw of the form of Jibril (peace be upon him). That is, his heart did not say, when he saw it: "I do not recognize you," for had it said that, it would have been lying, because he recognized him. The meaning is that he saw him with his eyes and recognized him with his heart, and he did not doubt that what he saw was true. It is also read *mā kadhaba*, meaning that he confirmed it, and did not doubt that it was Jibril (peace be upon him) in his form.

﴿Will you dispute with him what he saw?﴾: from *al-mirā'*, which is contention and argument. Its derivation is from *maraya al-nāqa* (he milked the she-camel), as if each of the two disputants milks what is with his companion. It is also read *afa-tamrūnahu*, meaning: will you overcome him in disputation, from *mārayatuhu fa-maraytuhu*. Because of the meaning of victory in it, it is construed with *'alā*, as you say "I overcame him in such-and-such." It is also said that *afa-tamrūnahu* means: will you deny him. They have recited:

*If you revile a brother of truth and nobility, you have indeed milked a brother who was not one to be milked by you.* [He says to his companion: if you blame a brother of truth and nobility, meaning himself. It is said: *maraya al-nāqa*, meaning he milked her. From this comes *al-mirā'*, as if each of the two disputants milks what is with his companion. From it: "you have indeed contended with a brother of truth," meaning you overcame him in dispute and drew out what was with him, because whoever milks a she-camel leaves her udder dry, or you denied his right as if you had taken it from him, or you caused what was with him to come out, so he blames you as you blamed him. *Mā kāna yumrīka*, meaning: what he did not do to you like that.]

They also said: it is said *mariyatuhu ḥaqqahu* when you deny it. Its construction with *'alā* is valid only according to the doctrine of implication (*taḍmīn*).

﴿Another descent﴾: a second time of descending. The word *nazla* is put in the accusative in the manner of the adverb of time, which is "once", because the form *fa'la* is a noun for the single occurrence of the verb, so it has its ruling. That is: Jibril (peace be upon him) descended upon him a second descent in his own form, and he saw him in it. That was on the night of the Ascension (*mi'rāj*).

It is said about the Lote-tree of the Utmost Boundary (*sidrat al-muntahā*): it is a jujube tree in the seventh heaven, to the right of the Throne. Its fruit is like the jars of Hajar, and its leaves are like the ears of elephants. From its root flow the rivers which Allah mentioned in His Book. A rider walks in its shade for seventy years without crossing it.

*Al-muntahā* means the place of ending, or the ending itself, as if it were at the furthest limit and end of Paradise. It is also said: no one has passed beyond it, and to it the knowledge of the angels and others ends, and no one knows what is beyond it. It is also said: the spirits of the martyrs terminate there.

﴿The Garden of Refuge﴾: the Garden to which the God-fearing go. Thus related al-Hasan. It is also said: the spirits of the martyrs take refuge in it.

And Ali and Ibn al-Zubayr and a group [of readers] recited: jannatu l-ma'wa (the Garden of Refuge), meaning: it covered it with its shadows and entered into it. It is reported from Aisha that she rejected this reading and said: "Whoever recites it that way, may God cover him [with a curse]." [Cf. the Arabic phrase: fa-ajannahu Allah.] "...what covered it" is an expression of magnification and amplification of what covered it. By this expression it is known that what covered it of creatures indicating the greatness and majesty of God are things that description cannot fathom and attribute cannot encompass. It has also been said: a vast multitude of angels covered it, worshipping God in its presence. And it is reported from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "I saw on every leaf of it an angel standing, glorifying God." [Narrated by al-Tabari through the route of Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: it was said to him, "O Messenger of God, what did you see covering that tree?" and he mentioned it and completed it more than this. But Abd al-Rahman is weak, and this report is mu'dal (with two or more consecutive omissions in its chain).] And from him, peace be upon him: it was covered by a canopy (rafraf) of green birds. [I have not found it.] And from Ibn Mas'ud and others: it was covered by golden butterflies (farash min dhahab). [As for the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh narrated it through the route of Murrah from him with this wording and more. As for others, it was narrated by [blank space in the original].]

"His gaze did not swerve, nor did it transgress" (ma zaagha basaru Rasul Allah (ﷺ) wa ma taghaa): that is, he affirmed what he saw with certain and correct affirmation, without his gaze deviating from it or passing beyond it; or: he did not turn away from the wonders he was commanded to see and was enabled to see, and "nor did it transgress" means he did not go beyond what he was commanded to see.

"Indeed he saw of the signs of his Lord the greatest signs" (La-qad ra'a min ayati Rabbihi al-kubra): by God, he indeed saw of the signs of his Lord the signs that are greatest and most magnificent. [Mahmud said: "its meaning is: he indeed saw of the signs of his Lord the signs which..." etc. Ahmad says: It is possible that "the greatest" is an attribute of "signs of his Lord," not a direct object, and the seen object is omitted for magnifying and glorifying the matter, as if he said: "He indeed saw of the greatest signs of his Lord matters of great magnitude that description cannot encompass," and omission in such a case is more eloquent and awe-inspiring. This—and God knows best—is preferable to the first, because in it there is magnification of God's greatest signs, and that among them are what he saw and what he did not see. On the first interpretation, its implication would be that he saw all the greatest signs in totality and generality, and this is far-fetched, for no one can comprehensively know the totality of God's signs. If one says: it is a general term intended as a particular, then it returns to the interpretation we mentioned, and God knows best.]

That is, when he ascended to his Lord to the heavens, and was shown the wonders of the dominion (malakut).

The Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat: idols that they had, and they are feminine. Al-Lat belonged to Thaqif at al-Ta'if.

It was said: it was at Nakhla, which Quraysh worshipped. It is on the pattern *fa'lah* from *lawa* (to turn, to bend), because they used to turn toward it and cling to it (*ya'kifun*) for worship, or they used to circle around it (*yaltawun 'alayha*), i.e., they would go around it (*yatufun*).

[[Mahmud said: "The derivation of al-Lat from *lawa 'ala kadha*, meaning to stand over something, because they used to..." etc. Ahmad said: *al-Ukhra* is the feminine of *akhar* (other). Undoubtedly it is in origin derived from posteriority in existence (*al-ta'khir al-wujudi*), but the Arabs shifted it from usage for posteriority in existence to usage where a different mention has come before, and nothing more, until it lost its original indicative meaning. This differs from *akhar* and *akhirah*, on the pattern *fa'il* and *fa'ilah*, whose implication of posteriority in existence remains unchanged. For this reason they avoided saying *rabi' al-akhar* on the pattern *af'al*, and *jumada al-ukhra*, and instead said *rabi' al-akhir* on the pattern *fa'il*, and *jumada al-akhirah* on the pattern *fa'ilah*, because they wanted to convey posteriority in existence, and the *af'al* and *fa'la* of this derivation have lost their indication of their purpose, so they shifted to *akhar* and *akhirah* and kept to them in both. This investigation is one that Shaykh Abu 'Amr ibn al-Hajib, may God have mercy on him, had clarified at the end of his life, and it is the truth, God willing. In that case the intended meaning is indicating the precedence of a different thing in mention, together with what we believe concerning the fulfilment of the verse-ending (*fasilah ra's al-ayah*). And God knows best.]]

It is also read *al-Lat* with a shadda (doubled *t*). They claimed that it was named after a man who used to knead (*yultu*) ghee with oil there and feed it to the pilgrims. From Mujahid: a man used to knead (*yultu*) sawiq (a porridge of grain) at al-Ta'if, and they used to cling to his grave, so they made him an idol.

Al-'Uzza belonged to Ghatafan, and it was an acacia tree (*samurah*). Its origin is the feminine of *a'azz* (mightier). The Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to it, and he cut it down. From it emerged a demoness (*shaytanah*), with disheveled hair, calling out and striking her face, placing her hand on her head. Khalid kept striking her with the sword until he killed her, saying:

"O 'Uzza, your disbelief! No glorification for you!
Indeed I have seen that God has humiliated you."

[[By Khalid ibn al-Walid, may God be pleased with him. *'Azz* is a truncated form (*murakhkham*) of *'Uzza*. Its truncation is anomalous (*shadhdh*), because it is neither quadriliteral nor feminine with a *ha'*. It is a tree that the Jahiliyyah used to worship. He struck it with his sword and a screaming jinn came out of it, and he said to her: "That is the confusion." It was also said: he struck it with an axe until he cut it down and killed the jinniyyah. *Kufranaka* is in the accusative by a necessarily omitted verb, like *subhanaka*: meaning "I disbelieve in you with a disbelief," not "I glorify you with glorification." The two are verbal nouns (*masadir*) that replace the utterance of their verbs. *Al-ihanah* means humiliation.]] He returned and informed the Messenger of God (ﷺ), who said, "That is al-'Uzza, and she will never be worshipped again."

[[Ibn Mardawayh narrated through Muhammad ibn Ishaq from Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi from Abu Salih, and from Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas, that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to al-'Uzza to demolish it. It was at Nakhla, and it had a custodian (*sadin*). Khalid came to it and demolished it, and he mentioned something similar to its end. Al-Waqidi in *al-Maghazi* and al-Azraqi in *al-Tarikh* narrated it through his chain, from 'Abdullah ibn Yazid al-Hudhali, from Sa'id ibn 'Amr al-Hudhali, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to Makkah," and mentioned the story, in which: "Khalid ibn al-Walid was sent to al-'Uzza to demolish it," and he mentioned the story. Ibn Sa'd likewise mentioned it in *al-Tabaqat* in the section on expeditions. The origin of this story was narrated by al-Nasa'i, Abu Ya'la, al-Tabarani, and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Dala'il*, from the hadith of Abu al-Tufayl, who said: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) conquered Makkah, he sent Khalid ibn al-Walid to Nakhla, where al-'Uzza was. Khalid came to it, and it was upon three trees, so he cut down the trees."]].

Manat was a rock that belonged to Hudhayl and Khuza'a. From Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both: it belonged to Thaqif. It is also read *Manah* (with a *hamzah*, *Manah*), and it seems it was named Manat because the blood of sacrifices used to be poured (*tumna*) at it, i.e., spilled. *Manah* is on the pattern *maf'alah* from *al-nau'* (rising of the stars), as if they used to seek rain from the rising of the stars at it, seeking blessing through it.

*Al-Ukhra* is a term of disparagement; it means the latest and lowest in rank, as in His statement: ﴿Their followers will say to their leaders﴾ (7:38), meaning their lowly ones to their chiefs and nobles.

It is possible that the priority and precedence among them belonged to al-Lat and al-'Uzza. They used to say that the angels and these idols were the daughters of God, and they worshipped them, claiming that they were their intercessors with God, while they buried their daughters alive. So it was said to them: ﴿Is it for you the male and for Him the female?﴾ (53:21).

It is also possible that what is meant is: al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat are females, and you have made them associates with God, and it is your nature to belittle females and disdain that they should be born to you and be attributed to you. How then do you make these females equals of God and name them gods? ﴿That is an unjust division﴾ (53:22), i.e., unjust, from *daza'ahu yadhazuhu*, meaning if he oppressed him. The original is *dawza*, and what was done to it was done to *bayd* so that the *ya'* would be preserved (*li-taslama al-ya'*). It is also read *di'za*, from *da'azahu* with a *hamzah*. And *Diz* with a *fathah* on the *dad*.

﴿It is nothing but names﴾ (53:23): it refers to the idols, meaning they are only names with no referents in reality, because you claim divinity for something that is farthest from it and most contrary to it. Similar to His statement: ﴿You worship besides Him only names that you have named﴾ (12:40). Or it refers to the names, which is their saying: al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat, and they intend by these names the gods. The meaning: these names are only names that you have named according to your whims and desires, and you have no proof from God for the validity of their naming that you can rely upon. The meaning of *sammaytumuha* is "you named them," as one says *sammaytuhu Zaydan* and *sammaytuhu bi-Zayd*. ﴿They follow only conjecture﴾ (53:23) is also read with a *ta'* (*tattabi'una*). It is only the supposition that what they are upon is true, that their gods are their intercessors, and what their souls desire, while they abandon what came to them of guidance and the evidence that their religion is false.

This is the commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 53, verse 26:

It means: the matter of intercession is restricted, for the angels, despite their nearness (to God), their high station, their multitude, and the heavens being crowded with their hosts, if they were to intercede all together for anyone, their intercession would not avail that person anything at all, and would not benefit him, except after God gives them leave to intercede for whomever He wills and approves, and sees as worthy of being interceded for. How then could idols intercede with Him on behalf of their worshippers? [[The phrase "bi-abadatihim" is probably "li-abadatihim" (for their worshippers), as in the wording of al-Nasafi. (ʿAyn)]]

They name the angels with the name of females, that is, each one of them, because when they say "the angels are daughters of God," they have named each of them a daughter, and this is naming them with the name of females. They have no knowledge of it, that is, of that and of what they say [[The author's note: "perhaps 'or what they say'." (A)]].

In the reading of Ubayy: "by it," that is, by the angels. Or: the naming does not avail anything against the truth. He means that the truth, which is the reality of a thing and what it is in itself, is grasped only through knowledge and certainty, not through conjecture and imagination.

So turn away from whoever you see turning away from the remembrance of God, who desires nothing but the life of this world and does not seek the Hereafter, and do not exhaust yourself over his acceptance of Islam. Then He said: "Indeed your Lord knows best," that is, only God knows who will respond and who will not respond, and you do not know. So ease your mind and do not trouble yourself, for you cannot guide whomever you love, and your duty is only to convey the message. His saying, exalted is He, "That is the extent of their knowledge," is either a parenthetical remark, or [it means] "so turn away from them and do not confront them." "Indeed your Lord knows best who has strayed from His path and who is guided," and He will recompense both of them with what they deserve of reward.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 53, verse 31–32:

It was read: *liyajziya* and *yujza*, with the yā' and the nūn in both. Its meaning is that Allah, mighty and majestic, only created the world and arranged these dominions (malakūt) for this purpose: that the good-doer among the responsible persons (mukallafīn) be recompensed, and the evil-doer among them likewise.

It is permissible for it to be connected to His saying, ﴿He knows best who has strayed from His way, and He knows best who is guided﴾, because the result of knowing the one who strays and the one who is guided is their recompense, ﴿for what they did﴾, meaning the punishment for what they did of evil, and ﴿with the best﴾, meaning with the best reward, which is the Garden. Or [it means] by reason of what they did of evil and by reason of the good deeds. ﴿The major sins of the wrongdoing﴾, i.e., the major sins from among the wrongdoing, because "ithm" (wrongdoing) is a genus that includes major and minor sins, and the major sins are the sins whose punishment is not removed except by repentance. It has been said: those whose punishment is great in comparison with the reward of their doer. ﴿And the indecencies﴾: what is grievously indecent among the major sins, as if he said: and the indecencies among them in particular. It was read: *kabīra al-ithm* (the great type of it), i.e., the great kind of it. It has been said: it is associating partners with Allah. And *al-lamam*: what is little and small. From it: *al-lamam* is touching of madness, and the slight insanity from it.

And he "alamma bi-l-makān" when his staying in the place is brief. And he "alamma bi-l-ṭaʿām": he ate little of it. From it is the verse:

*Liqāʾ akhillāʾ al-ṣafāʾ li-mām ... wa-kull wiṣāl al-ghāniyāt dhimām*

i.e., the meeting of the beloved friends whose affection is pure is *limām*, meaning little, so it is a *mufāʿala* from *al-ilmām*, which is an increase without staying or dwelling; and all union with women who are self-sufficient through their beauty, needing no adornment with jewelry, or the veiled ones who remain in their houses, from *ghaniya bi-l-makān* like *riḍiya*: he stayed in the place, *dhimām* meaning a small amount of the rights of sanctity and covenant. The intended meaning is minor sins. The words of the Exalted, ﴿except the minor lapses﴾, are either an exceptive connection (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ) or a qualifier, like His saying, ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah﴾: as if it were said: the major sins of wrongdoing other than minor lapses, and gods other than Allah. From Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī: the *lamam* is the glance, the wink, and the kiss. From al-Suddī: the passing thought of sin. From al-Kalbī: every sin for which Allah has not mentioned a prescribed penalty or punishment. From ʿAṭāʾ: the habit of the soul from time to time. ﴿Indeed your Lord is vast in forgiveness﴾, where He removes minor sins by avoiding major ones,[[The statement "He removes minor sins by avoiding major ones" is the view of the Muʿtazila; according to the people of the Sunna, it is so, or it is by bare grace; and likewise what follows. (ʿ)]] and major sins by repentance. ﴿So do not claim purity for yourselves﴾: do not attribute them to purity of deed, increase of goodness, and performing acts of obedience, or to purity and cleanness from disobedience; do not praise them and do not exalt them. Allah has known the pure among you and the pious, first and last, before He brought you forth from the loins of Adam, and before you came out from the bellies of your mothers. It has been said: some people would do good deeds and then say, "Our prayer, our fasting, our pilgrimage," so this was revealed. This applies when it is out of self-admiration or showing off. As for one who believes that the righteous deed he performed is from Allah, by His enabling and support, and did not intend self-praise, he is not among those who purify themselves, because joy in obedience is itself obedience, and mentioning it is gratitude.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 53, verse 31–32:

It was read: *liyajziya* and *yujza*, with the yā' and the nūn in both. Its meaning is that Allah, mighty and majestic, only created the world and arranged these dominions (malakūt) for this purpose: that the good-doer among the responsible persons (mukallafīn) be recompensed, and the evil-doer among them likewise.

It is permissible for it to be connected to His saying, ﴿He knows best who has strayed from His way, and He knows best who is guided﴾, because the result of knowing the one who strays and the one who is guided is their recompense, ﴿for what they did﴾, meaning the punishment for what they did of evil, and ﴿with the best﴾, meaning with the best reward, which is the Garden. Or [it means] by reason of what they did of evil and by reason of the good deeds. ﴿The major sins of the wrongdoing﴾, i.e., the major sins from among the wrongdoing, because "ithm" (wrongdoing) is a genus that includes major and minor sins, and the major sins are the sins whose punishment is not removed except by repentance. It has been said: those whose punishment is great in comparison with the reward of their doer. ﴿And the indecencies﴾: what is grievously indecent among the major sins, as if he said: and the indecencies among them in particular. It was read: *kabīra al-ithm* (the great type of it), i.e., the great kind of it. It has been said: it is associating partners with Allah. And *al-lamam*: what is little and small. From it: *al-lamam* is touching of madness, and the slight insanity from it.

And he "alamma bi-l-makān" when his staying in the place is brief. And he "alamma bi-l-ṭaʿām": he ate little of it. From it is the verse:

*Liqāʾ akhillāʾ al-ṣafāʾ li-mām ... wa-kull wiṣāl al-ghāniyāt dhimām*

(ʿ)]] and major sins by repentance. ﴿So do not claim purity for yourselves﴾: do not attribute them to purity of deed, increase of goodness, and performing acts of obedience, or to purity and cleanness from disobedience; do not praise them and do not exalt them. **Akdā** means he cut off his giving and withheld it. Its root is *ikdāʾ al-ḥāfir*, which is when the digger strikes a *kudya*, a hardness like a rock, and so stops digging. It is related that ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with him, used to give away his wealth in good causes. His half-brother through nursing, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Saʿd ibn Abī Sarḥ, said to him: "Soon nothing will be left for you." ʿUthmān replied: "I have sins and misdeeds, and by what I do I seek the pleasure of Allah the Exalted and hope for His pardon." ʿAbd Allāh said: "Give me your she-camel with its saddle, and I will bear all your sins for you." So ʿUthmān gave it to him, had it witnessed, and withheld his giving. Then this was revealed.

**Tawallā** means he abandoned his post on the day of Uḥud. ʿUthmān then returned to something better and finer than that. **Fa-huwa yarā**, that is, he knows that what his brother said about bearing his burdens is true. **Waffā** is read with a light and with a heavy pronunciation. The heavy form is an intensification of fulfilment. Or it means *wafara wa-atamma* (he filled out and completed), as in Allah's words ﴿and He completed them﴾. Its meaning is general, to cover every fulfilment and full performance. Among these: his conveying of the message, his bearing alone the burdens of prophethood, his patience in being willing to sacrifice his son and in the fire of Nimrod, his care for his guests and his serving them with his own hands. He used to go out every day and walk a farsakh (about three miles) in search of a guest; if he found one he honoured him, and if not he intended to fast.

From al-Ḥasan: he was never commanded by Allah to do anything without fulfilling it.

From al-Hazīl ibn Sharaḥbīl [[The phrase "from al-Hazīl ibn Sharaḥbīl" is probably "al-Hudhayl." (ʿ)]]: between Nūḥ and Ibrāhīm, a man would be seized for the offence of another, and would be killed for his father, son, paternal uncle or maternal uncle; a husband for his wife, and a slave for his master. The first to oppose them was Ibrāhīm.

From ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib: he made a covenant not to ask anything of any created being. When he was thrown into the fire, Jibrīl and Mīkāʾīl said to him: "Do you have any need?" He said: "As for you two, no."

From the Prophet ﷺ: in his practice each day, four rakʿas at the beginning of the day, which is the prayer of ḍuḥā (forenoon).[[Reported by al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim and others, from the narration of Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr, from al-Qāsim, from Abū Umāma, as a marfūʿ report, and fuller than this.]]

It is also related: "Shall I not tell you why Allah named His friend ﴿who fulfilled﴾? He used to say when he woke in the morning and when he reached evening: ﴿So glory be to Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ … up to ﴿and when you emerge﴾."[[Reported by Aḥmad, al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn al-Sunnī, al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Abī Ḥātim, from the narration of Ibn Lahīʿa, from Ziyād, from Ziyān, from Ibn Fāʾid, from Sahl ibn Muʿādh, from his father, as a marfūʿ report.]]

It is also said: "﴿Who fulfilled﴾ refers to the portions of Islam, which are thirty: ten in the chapter of Repentance, ﴿those who repent﴾; ten in the chapter of the Confederates, ﴿indeed the Muslim men﴾; and ten in the chapter of the Believers, ﴿the believers have indeed prospered﴾."

It is read **fī ṣuḥuf** with the light form. **Allā tazir** is *an* in its light form, from the heavy form. The meaning is: that no bearer of burdens shall bear, and the pronoun is the pronoun of the matter. The position of *an* and what follows it is in the genitive, as an appositive to *mā fī ṣuḥuf Mūsā* (what is in the scrolls of Mūsā). Or it is in the nominative, as if someone had said: "What is in the scrolls of Mūsā and Ibrāhīm?" and it was answered: *an lā tazir* (that no bearer of burdens shall bear) ﴿except what he strove for﴾, that is, except his own striving.

If you ask: is it not established in the reports that giving charity on behalf of the dead, performing Ḥajj on their behalf, and the multiplication of reward (*al-iḍʿāf*) benefit them? I answer: there are two replies. The first is that the striving of another does not benefit a person except when it is built upon his own striving, which means that he is a believing and righteous person. Likewise the multiplication: the striving of another is treated as his own striving, because it follows him and stands by his standing. The second is that the striving of another does not benefit him when it is done for himself, but when it is intended on his behalf, it is by the ruling of the Sharīʿa like a deputy for him and an agent standing in his place.

**Thumma yujzāhu**, then the servant is recompensed for his striving. One says *jazāhu Allāhu ʿamalahu* and *jazāhu ʿalā ʿamalihi*, with the preposition omitted and the verb made to reach its object. It is permissible that the pronoun refers to the recompense; then he explains it with ﴿the fullest recompense﴾, or it is a substitute for it, like Allah's words ﴿and the wrongdoers conspired in secret﴾.

﴿And that to your Lord is the final end﴾ is read with the fatḥa, meaning that all of this is in the scrolls. It is read with the kasra, as a new sentence, and likewise what follows it. **Al-muntahā** is a verbal noun meaning the arriving: creation arrives at Him and returns to Him, like Allah's words ﴿to Allah is the final destination﴾.

﴿And He causes laughter and weeping﴾: He created the faculties of laughing and weeping.[[Maḥmūd said: "That is, He created the faculties of laughing and weeping." Aḥmad said: He also created laughing and weeping according to the principles of the Sunna (the prophetic tradition, understood by Ahl al-Sunna as the normative basis of belief), and the verse indicates this, without distorting it. And Allah is the Granter of success.]]

﴿When it is emitted﴾: when it is poured forth into the womb. One says *manā* and *amnā*.

From al-Akhfash: "He is created from the *manī* (semen) of the one who measures," that is, the one who decrees.

﴿The creation of the second existence﴾ is read *al-nashʾa* and *al-nashāʾa* with the long vowel.

He said ﴿upon Him﴾ [ʿalayhi] because it is obligatory upon Him, in wisdom,[[Maḥmūd said: "He only said ʿalayhi because it is obligatory upon Him…" etc. Aḥmad said: this is from the corruption of the belief of the Muʿtazila, whom they call "consideration of what is good and wise." What corruption could be greater than what leads to the Muʿtazila belief that obligation is laid upon the Lord of lords, exalted be Allah above that. A principle such as this, whose decisive proofs have been effaced and whose ruling annulled, cannot be upheld by an ambiguous word. If it were clear, it would have to be interpreted in a way that reconciles it with the decisive texts. ﴿And He enriches and grants possessions﴾: He gave *qinya*, which is the wealth that you have accumulated and resolved not to let go from your hand.

﴿The Sirius, Lord of the Constellation Jawzāʾ﴾: it is the star that rises after it, and it is called the Hound of the Giant (*kalb al-Jabbār*). It is read ʿĀdan Lūlā and ʿĀdun Lūlā, with the tanwīn assimilated into the lām and the hamza of *ūlā* dropped, its vowel transferred to the lām of the definite article.

A similar form is *ajbal al-ḥāfir*. It was then used figuratively: *ajbal al-shāʿir* means the poet became tongue-tied when he could not continue.

It is related that ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with him, used to give away his wealth in good causes. So ʿUthmān gave it to him, had it witnessed, and withheld his giving. Then this was revealed.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 53, verses 59–62:

﴿Do you then marvel at this discourse﴾, meaning the Qur'an, in denial, ﴿and laugh﴾ in mockery, ﴿and not weep﴾? Weeping and humble submission are obligatory upon you.

It is related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he was never seen laughing after this surah was revealed.¹

It is also recited as ﻿تعجبون تضحكون﻿ (ta'jabūna tadhakūna), without the waw (و) before the second verb.² ﴿While you are sāmidūn﴾, meaning haughty and proud (shāmikhūn, mubarṭimūn).³

It has been said: "lāhūn lā'ibūn," meaning heedless and playing. Some of them said to his slave-girl: "Usmudī lanā," meaning: sing for us. ﴿So prostrate yourselves to Allah and worship﴾, and do not worship the gods.

It is related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Najm, Allah will grant him ten good deeds for each person who believed in Muhammad and denied him in Makkah."⁴

---

¹ Related by Aḥmad in *al-Zuhd* and by al-Tha'labī from the hadith of Ṣāliḥ ibn Abī al-Khalīl. Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through Sa'īd ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbās with a weak chain of transmission.

² Al-Zamakhsharī's remark on the reading here concerns the variant in which the waw is omitted.

³ His statement "shāmikhūn mubarṭimūn" is explained in *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* (by al-Jawharī): "al-barṭamah" is swelling from anger. Also in that work: "al-sāmid" is one who raises his head in arrogance; one who is heedless; one who is standing; one who is silent; and one who is sorrowful and humble. "Isma'adda al-rajul" (with a hamza) means the man swelled with anger.

⁴ Related by al-Tha'labī, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Wāḥidī from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 53, verses 59–62:

﴿Do you then marvel at this discourse﴾, meaning the Qur'an, in denial, ﴿and laugh﴾ in mockery, ﴿and not weep﴾? Weeping and humble submission are obligatory upon you.

It is related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he was never seen laughing after this surah was revealed.¹

It is also recited as ﻿تعجبون تضحكون﻿ (ta'jabūna tadhakūna), without the waw (و) before the second verb.² ﴿While you are sāmidūn﴾, meaning haughty and proud (shāmikhūn, mubarṭimūn).³

It has been said: "lāhūn lā'ibūn," meaning heedless and playing. Some of them said to his slave-girl: "Usmudī lanā," meaning: sing for us. ﴿So prostrate yourselves to Allah and worship﴾, and do not worship the gods.

It is related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Najm, Allah will grant him ten good deeds for each person who believed in Muhammad and denied him in Makkah."⁴

---

¹ Related by Aḥmad in *al-Zuhd* and by al-Tha'labī from the hadith of Ṣāliḥ ibn Abī al-Khalīl. Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through Sa'īd ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbās with a weak chain of transmission.

² Al-Zamakhsharī's remark on the reading here concerns the variant in which the waw is omitted.

³ His statement "shāmikhūn mubarṭimūn" is explained in *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* (by al-Jawharī): "al-barṭamah" is swelling from anger. Also in that work: "al-sāmid" is one who raises his head in arrogance; one who is heedless; one who is standing; one who is silent; and one who is sorrowful and humble. "Isma'adda al-rajul" (with a hamza) means the man swelled with anger.

⁴ Related by al-Tha'labī, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Wāḥidī from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him.
